articles.title: What is BTPM?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: BTPM is a business transformation project management tool for structured execution, governance, reporting, and traceability.
articles.summary: BTPM helps teams manage transformation work through projects, phases, tasks, risks, blockers, KPIs, governance, files, and reporting outputs.
articles.body:
BTPM is a project management and governance tool for business transformation work.

It helps teams keep project execution, governance, and reporting in one controlled place. Instead of managing work only through emails, spreadsheets, meetings, and scattered files, BTPM gives the team a structured way to define work, assign ownership, track progress, manage risks, record governance evidence, and produce reporting outputs.

BTPM is useful when work needs more structure than a simple task list. For example, use it when a project has phases, owners, timelines, KPIs, risks, blockers, governance reviews, or management reporting needs.

In BTPM, the live project record should stay in BTPM. Reports, PowerPoint decks, SharePoint files, Power BI dashboards, and exported documents are downstream outputs or supporting tools. They should not become a separate version of the truth.

BTPM does not replace every tool. Outlook and Teams still handle meetings and communication. SharePoint stores documents. Power BI supports reporting. BTPM connects the project structure, execution record, governance evidence, and source data.

What is BTPM used for?
Is BTPM a project management tool?

answer_rules: Explain BTPM as a project management and governance tool for business transformation.
Say BTPM is the live project record.
Clarify that SharePoint, Power BI, Teams, Outlook, and exports are supporting or downstream tools.
forbidden_claims: BTPM replaces every business tool.
Power BI or SharePoint is the live project record.
BTPM automatically manages meetings and communication.

articles.title: Understanding the BTPM structure
articles.tooltip_excerpt: BTPM is organized around workspaces, programs, projects, phases, tasks, and supporting governance objects.
articles.summary: The BTPM structure helps users understand where work belongs: workspace, program, project, phase, task, risk, blocker, KPI, governance record, file, or report output.
articles.body:
BTPM is structured so work can be organized clearly.

The main structure is:

- Organization: the overall company or tenant.
- Workspace: a working area for a team, function, or portfolio.
- Program: a group of related projects, where used.
- Project: a governed delivery effort with ownership, timeline, and reporting.
- Phase: a major stage of a project.
- Task: a specific executable work item inside a phase.

Supporting objects help manage the project:

- Risks: future threats that may affect the project.
- Blockers: current issues already stopping progress.
- KPIs: measurable indicators with targets and update history.
- Governance cadences and records: expected reviews and evidence that they happened.
- Files and generated documents: supporting outputs and documents.
- Comments and execution updates: discussion and dated progress history.

Use the structure to decide where information belongs. A project should not become one large notes page, and a task should not be used to hide a multi-week initiative.

If you are unsure where to record something, ask: “Is this a project, a phase of delivery, a specific action, a risk, a blocker, a KPI, or governance evidence?”

question_examples: How is BTPM structured?
What is the difference between workspace, program, project, phase, and task?
Where should I record project information?
What are supporting objects in BTPM?
answer_rules: Explain the structure in simple hierarchy terms.
Mention supporting objects such as risks, blockers, KPIs, governance, files, comments, and execution updates.
Help users decide where information belongs.
forbidden_claims: Tasks should contain entire multi-week projects.
All information should be kept in the project overview.
Files are the live project structure.

articles.title: Program, project, phase, and task rulebook
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Use programs, projects, phases, and tasks consistently so BTPM reporting and ownership stay clear.
articles.summary: Programs group related projects. Projects are governed delivery efforts. Phases are major project stages. Tasks are specific work items that can be assigned and completed.
articles.body:
Use the BTPM hierarchy consistently.

A program groups related projects. Use it when several projects contribute to a broader business outcome, portfolio, or initiative.

A project is a governed delivery effort. It usually has an owner, timeline, status, risks, blockers, KPIs, governance needs, and reporting expectations.

A phase is a major stage inside a project. Examples include Discovery, Design, Build, Testing, Training, Go-Live, or Closure. A phase helps structure the project timeline.

A task is a specific work item inside a phase. It should be clear enough that someone can own it, update it, and mark it complete.

Simple rule:

- Program = group of related projects.
- Project = governed delivery effort.
- Phase = major stage of the project.
- Task = specific action inside a phase.

Avoid two common mistakes:

1. Do not create a new project for every small action.
2. Do not hide a real project inside one task.

Good structure makes reporting easier. It also helps users understand ownership, deadlines, dependencies, and what needs attention.

question_examples: What is the difference between program, project, phase, and task?
When should I use a program?
Is this a project or a task?
What is a phase?
answer_rules: Define each level clearly and practically.
Warn against creating projects for small actions or hiding projects inside tasks.
Link the structure to ownership and reporting.
forbidden_claims: Program, project, phase, and task mean the same thing.
Every task should become a project.
A full project should be managed as one task.

articles.title: Task types rulebook
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Task types help clarify the nature of work, but every task should still have a clear owner, expected outcome, and completion point.
articles.summary: Use task types to make project work easier to understand. A task should be specific, actionable, and clear enough to update or complete.
articles.body:
A task is a specific work item inside a project phase.

Task types can help clarify what kind of work is being managed. Depending on the project setup, a task may represent delivery work, review work, decision work, approval work, documentation, testing, training, follow-up, or another practical activity.

The exact type matters less than the quality of the task.

A good task should have:

- a clear action;
- an owner or responsible person;
- a due date or expected timing;
- a status;
- enough context for another user to understand it;
- a clear completion point.

Avoid vague tasks such as “Follow up,” “Discuss,” or “Work on project” unless the description makes the expected outcome clear.

A better task says what needs to happen:

- “Confirm UAT participants”
- “Approve training material”
- “Validate migration checklist”
- “Prepare SteerCo status deck”

Use task types to improve clarity, not to create unnecessary administration. If the task is simple, keep it simple.

question_examples: What are task types?
What makes a good task?
How should I write a task?
Should every task be detailed?
answer_rules: Explain that task types support clarity.
Emphasize owner, action, due date, status, and completion point.
Warn against vague task titles.
forbidden_claims: Task type is more important than task clarity.
Every simple task needs heavy administration.
Vague tasks are sufficient without context.

articles.title: Dependencies rulebook
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Use dependencies when one item must wait for another before it can start or finish.
articles.summary: Dependencies explain sequencing. They help users understand what work depends on something else and where delays may affect the plan.
articles.body:
A dependency means one item depends on another item before it can start, continue, or finish.

Use dependencies when the sequence matters. For example:

- UAT cannot start until the test environment is ready.
- Training cannot be finalized until the process design is approved.
- Go-live cannot happen until critical defects are resolved.
- A report cannot be submitted until KPI values are updated.

Dependencies are useful because they show where a delay may affect other work. They also help the team understand why one task cannot move forward yet.

Do not create dependencies for every loose relationship. If two tasks are related but one does not actually block the other, a comment or description may be enough.

A good dependency answers:

- What is waiting?
- What is it waiting for?
- What happens if the predecessor is delayed?
- Who owns the next action?

Dependencies are not only visual. They should reflect real sequencing logic in the project plan.

When should I add a dependency?
Are dependencies only visual?

answer_rules: Explain dependency as real sequencing logic.
Tell users not to create dependencies for every loose relationship.
Link dependencies to schedule impact and ownership.
forbidden_claims: Dependencies are only visual.
Every related task needs a dependency.
Dependencies do not affect planning.

articles.title: Risk vs blocker rulebook
articles.tooltip_excerpt: A risk is a possible future problem. A blocker is a current issue already stopping or materially delaying progress.
articles.summary: Use risks and blockers consistently. Risks need mitigation; blockers need removal or resolution so work can continue.
articles.body:
A risk is something that may happen and could affect the project.

A blocker is something that is already happening and is stopping or materially delaying progress.

Simple rule:

- Risk = possible future problem.
- Blocker = current issue already affecting execution.

Examples:

- Risk: "Key users may not be available for UAT."
- Blocker: "UAT cannot start because the test environment is unavailable."
- Risk: "Supplier confirmation may be late."
- Blocker: "Supplier confirmation is already overdue and the next task cannot start."

Use risks to manage uncertainty. The focus is mitigation: what can we do now to reduce the chance or impact?

Use blockers to manage immediate obstruction. The focus is removal: what must happen so work can continue?

Do not turn every concern into a blocker. That makes the blocker list noisy and reduces urgency. Also, do not leave real blockers hidden as risks. If progress is already stopped, it should be visible as a blocker.

question_examples: What is the difference between a risk and a blocker?
Should this be a risk or a blocker?
When should I create a blocker?
What should I do with a risk?
answer_rules: Define risk as a possible future problem.
Define blocker as a current issue already stopping or delaying progress.
Explain mitigation for risks and removal for blockers.
Warn against recording every concern as a blocker.
forbidden_claims: Risks and blockers are the same thing.
Every concern should be a blocker.
A blocker is only a possible future issue.

articles.title: Comment vs execution update rulebook
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Use comments for discussion. Use execution updates for dated progress records that explain what changed.
articles.summary: Comments and execution updates serve different purposes. Comments are conversational; execution updates are progress history.
articles.body:
Comments and execution updates should not be used the same way.

Use a comment for discussion, clarification, questions, or context. A comment is useful when people need to talk about the work.

Use an execution update when you need to record meaningful progress or a status change. An execution update should help someone understand what changed, when it changed, and what happens next.

Examples of comments:

- “Can you confirm who owns this?”
- “Please attach the latest file.”
- “This depends on supplier feedback.”

Examples of execution updates:

- “UAT script review completed. Two open comments remain.”
- “Training material sent to business owners for review.”
- “Go-live date moved because vendor confirmation is delayed.”

A simple rule:

- Comment = conversation.
- Execution update = progress history.

Do not use vague execution updates such as “working on it” if the team needs real information. A better update says what changed, what is next, and whether anything is blocked.

question_examples: What is the difference between a comment and an execution update?
When should I add an execution update?
Should I use a comment or a progress update?
Is “working on it” a good update?
answer_rules: Explain comment as conversation.
Explain execution update as dated progress history.
Encourage specific progress updates.
forbidden_claims: Comments and execution updates are the same.
“Working on it” is always enough as an execution update.
Comments are the official progress history.

articles.title: How to create phases and tasks
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Use phases for major stages of delivery and tasks for specific executable actions inside each phase.
articles.summary: Phases and tasks make a project executable. Phases organize the project journey; tasks define the specific work people own and update.
articles.body:
Create phases and tasks when you need to turn a project idea into an executable plan.

A phase is a major stage of the project. Examples include Discovery, Design, Build, Testing, Training, Go-Live, and Closure.

A task is a specific work item inside a phase. It should be clear enough that someone can own it, update it, and mark it complete.

How to structure the plan:

1. Start with the main delivery phases.
2. Add tasks under the correct phase.
3. Give each task a clear action-oriented title.
4. Assign an owner where possible.
5. Add dates or expected timing.
6. Add priority, status, or dependencies where useful.
7. Keep the plan clean and understandable.

Avoid vague tasks such as “follow up” or “work on implementation” unless the description explains the expected outcome.

A good task answers:

- What needs to happen?
- Who owns it?
- When is it expected?
- What does “done” mean?

Adoption Plan can generate or add Adoption tasks into Planning. Those tasks are still normal BTPM tasks.

After generation or add-from-template:
- edit task title, owner, status, priority, and dates in Planning
- view Adoption badges on Adoption-related tasks
- use the Adoption Plan tab to see Adoption tasks grouped by initiative
- use Manage adoption links to connect existing Planning tasks to the Adoption Plan

Do not create a separate Adoption task outside Planning. Planning remains the task source of truth.

synonyms: where do I edit adoption tasks

What is the difference between a phase and a task?
How should I structure a project plan?
What makes a task clear?
answer_rules: Explain phases as major project stages.
Explain tasks as specific executable work inside phases.
Encourage action-oriented task titles and clear completion points.
forbidden_claims: A task can replace a full project phase.
Vague task names are enough without context.
Every project should have the same phases.

articles.title: How to add a dependency
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Add a dependency when one task, phase, or milestone must wait for another before it can move forward.
articles.summary: Dependencies help explain real sequencing. Use them when work is waiting for another item, not just because two items are generally related.
articles.body:
Add a dependency when one item must wait for another before it can start, continue, or finish.

Exact steps in BTPM (verified UI):

1. Open the Task, Phase, or Project Overview for the item that should be blocked by another.
2. Scroll to the Dependencies panel (heading 'Dependencies').
3. In the predecessor dropdown, pick the same-level item that must finish first.
4. Click the 'Blocked by' button to add the dependency.
5. The new dependency appears under 'Blocked by' with an 'FS' (Finish-to-Start) badge. Remove it later with the X icon.

Permissions: this requires project planning authority (edit permission). If the Dependencies panel is read-only for you, ask a Workspace Admin.

Where this is not supported:

- The Gantt view only displays dependency arrows. It does not expose an Add/Remove control — create and edit dependencies from the Dependencies panel on the Task, Phase, or Project Overview page.
- Cross-level dependencies (project to task, phase to task) are not supported in v1. Only same-level Finish-to-Start dependencies are allowed.

When to add a dependency:

- testing cannot start until the environment is ready;
- training cannot be finalized until the process is approved;
- go-live cannot happen until critical defects are resolved;
- a report cannot be submitted until KPI values are updated.

Before adding a dependency, check: what is waiting, what is it waiting for, is the relationship truly blocking, what happens if the first item is delayed, and who owns the next action. Do not add dependencies for every loose relationship — use a comment, description, or execution update instead.

When should I use a dependency?

answer_rules: Explain dependency as real sequencing.
Tell users to avoid weak dependencies.
Mention schedule impact and ownership.
forbidden_claims: Every related task needs a dependency.
Dependencies are only decorative.
Dependencies should be used instead of clear task ownership.

articles.title: How to update task or phase execution
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Update execution when meaningful progress, a status change, a delay, or a decision needs to be recorded.
articles.summary: Execution updates help the team understand what changed, what is next, and whether anything is blocked. They should be clear and dated.
articles.body:
Update execution when there is meaningful progress or a relevant change.

Use execution updates to record:

- work completed;
- status changes;
- delays;
- decisions;
- blockers or dependencies;
- next steps;
- important context for future review.

A useful execution update should answer:

1. What changed?
2. When did it change?
3. What is next?
4. Is anything blocked?
5. Does anyone need to act?

Examples:

- “UAT script review completed. Two comments remain with Business Owner.”
- “Vendor confirmation delayed. Go-live planning cannot continue until confirmation is received.”
- “Training material approved. Next step is scheduling user sessions.”

Avoid vague updates such as:

- “working on it”
- “in progress”
- “followed up”

Those may be true, but they do not help the team understand progress.

Use comments for discussion. Use execution updates for progress history.

forbidden_claims: “Working on it” is always enough.

articles.title: How to manage risks and blockers
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Manage risks and blockers by assigning owners, keeping next actions clear, and closing items when they are resolved.
articles.summary: Risks and blockers are useful only when they are actively managed. Each item should have an owner, a clear next action, and regular updates.
articles.body:
Managing risks and blockers is not just about recording problems. The value comes from making the next action clear.

Use this workflow:

1. Decide whether the item is a risk or a blocker.
2. Write a clear title that explains the issue.
3. Add enough context so another person can understand the situation.
4. Assign an owner.
5. Set impact or priority where available.
6. Add mitigation, resolution steps, or the next action.
7. Review the item regularly.
8. Close or resolve it when it is no longer active.

For a risk, focus on mitigation. Ask: “What can we do now to reduce the chance or impact?”

For a blocker, focus on removal. Ask: “What must happen so work can continue?”

Do not leave old items open forever. If a risk is no longer relevant, close it. If a blocker has been removed, resolve it. Keeping the list clean helps project reviews focus on what really needs attention.

Risks and blockers can be linked to the Adoption Plan when they relate to adoption, stakeholder readiness, communication, training, or hypercare.

A linked risk or blocker remains a normal BTPM risk or blocker. It does not become a separate Adoption-only object. The Adoption relationship is shown through an Adoption badge or through the linked objects section in the Adoption Plan.

Use this when, for example:
- a stakeholder readiness issue is a risk
- training availability is a blocker
- communication delay affects adoption
- hypercare support is blocked

Continue editing the risk or blocker in Risks & Blockers.

articles.title: How to manage and update KPIs
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Update KPIs when a new measured value is available and the value belongs in the project KPI history.
articles.summary: KPI updates should record measured values clearly. Update the KPI in BTPM first, then use dashboards, snapshots, or reporting outputs from that source.
articles.body:
Update a KPI when a new measured value is available.

Before updating a KPI, check:

1. Is the KPI definition clear?
2. Are you updating the right KPI?
3. Is the value for the correct date or reporting period?
4. Is the unit of measure clear?
5. Does the value need a comment or explanation?
6. Is this part of an official snapshot or reporting process?

A good KPI update records the value and enough context for someone else to understand it later.

Do not use KPI updates for general comments. If the information is not measurable, it may belong in an execution update, risk, blocker, or governance record.

If the KPI is used in reporting, update BTPM first. Power BI, status decks, exported reports, and KPI App submission flows should consume controlled BTPM KPI data. They should not become a separate place where KPI truth is manually maintained.

BTPM Guide can explain how KPI updates work, but it cannot create KPI values or approve submissions for you.

KPIs can be linked to the Adoption Plan when they measure adoption or readiness.

Examples:
- training completion
- adoption percentage
- user readiness score
- feedback response rate
- hypercare issue closure rate
- stakeholder engagement completion

A linked KPI remains a normal BTPM KPI. KPI values and history are still managed in the KPI area. The Adoption Plan only shows the relationship so adoption-related measures are visible in context.

articles.title: Health, RAG, and schedule signal
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Health and schedule signals help users see whether a project looks safe, at risk, or off track.
articles.summary: Project health, RAG, and schedule signals are reporting indicators. They should help users understand whether the project needs attention, not replace project updates.
articles.body:
Health, RAG, and schedule signals help users understand whether a project looks safe, at risk, or off track.

A health signal usually answers: “Is the project situation okay?”

A schedule signal usually answers: “Does the timing look okay?”

RAG often means:

- Green: broadly on track.
- Amber: needs attention or has risk.
- Red: off track or needs urgent action.

These signals are useful because they give a quick management view. But they are not enough on their own. If a project is amber or red, users should be able to understand why by looking at tasks, dates, risks, blockers, KPIs, governance records, or execution updates.

Do not use red just because a project is active or busy. Red should mean there is a real issue that needs attention.

Do not use green to hide problems. If the project has serious blockers, overdue critical tasks, or missed governance, the health signal should reflect that.

forbidden_claims: Red means simply in progress.

articles.title: Roadmap and Gantt
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Roadmap is the cross-project view. Gantt is the project timeline view. Both should reflect BTPM project data.
articles.summary: Use Roadmap for portfolio or cross-project visibility. Use Gantt to understand the timeline of one project. Neither should become a separate source of truth.
articles.body:
Roadmap and Gantt are both timeline-related views, but they are used for different purposes.

The Roadmap is the cross-project view. Use it when you want to understand status, timing, health, or reporting across several projects, programs, or workspaces.

The Gantt is the project timeline view. Use it when you want to understand the sequence and timing of phases and tasks inside one project.

A simple rule:

- Roadmap = cross-project visibility.
- Gantt = one project’s timeline.

Both views should reflect BTPM project data. They should not become separate planning systems.

Use Roadmap when you need to answer:

- What is happening across the portfolio?
- Which projects are at risk?
- What should be included in a management update?
- What scope should be included in a Roadmap Status Deck?

Use Gantt when you need to answer:

- Are the project dates realistic?
- Which tasks depend on each other?
- What happens if one phase moves?

Explain Gantt as one project timeline.
State that both reflect BTPM project data and are not separate sources of truth.
forbidden_claims: Roadmap is a separate planning database.
Gantt is a separate project plan.
Roadmap and Gantt mean the same thing.

articles.title: How to set up SharePoint in Admin
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Org Admins configure the organization SharePoint site once, then assign and validate workspace libraries under that site.
articles.summary: Admin SharePoint has two real operational setup layers: the organization SharePoint site and workspace library assignments. Project-level SharePoint use depends on this setup.
articles.body:
Admin SharePoint is the Org Admin surface for configuring the SharePoint integration used by BTPM.

There are two separate setup layers:

1. Organization SharePoint site. Configure the organization-level SharePoint site once. This is the parent site used for workspace library assignments.

2. Workspace library assignments. Assign one SharePoint library to each workspace under the configured organization site. Workspace library assignment does not ask for a separate site URL; it uses the organization site.

Main operational actions:

1. Connect site. Use this when no organization SharePoint site is connected.
2. Validate site. Use this to check that BTPM can validate the configured site.
3. Disconnect site. Use this only when the organization site connection should be removed; workspace library assignments may become invalid until a new site is configured.
4. Assign or change workspace library. Use this per workspace after the organization site is connected.
5. Validate workspace library. Use this to check that the assigned library is reachable and valid.
6. Remove workspace library assignment. Use this when the workspace should no longer be linked to that SharePoint library.

Important boundaries:
- Admin SharePoint setup is different from project-level SharePoint file use.
- SharePoint permissions are still controlled by Microsoft/SharePoint and may need separate handling outside BTPM.
- BTPM project pages may show read-only SharePoint visibility based on the configured connection.
- Guide Mode can explain SharePoint setup but must not connect, validate, disconnect, assign, or remove SharePoint links on behalf of the user.

Connect a project to a SharePoint folder when the project needs a clear document location.

Connecting a folder does not mean SharePoint controls the project. BTPM remains the place to update project status, tasks, risks, blockers, KPIs, governance, and reporting source data.

If project information changes later, update BTPM first and generate a fresh charter. Do not manually edit an old charter and treat it as the live project record.

Use the charter to communicate the project clearly. Use BTPM to maintain the project truth.

articles.title: Why can’t I open a SharePoint folder or file?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: If SharePoint files won't open from BTPM, it is usually SharePoint permissions, the wrong Microsoft account, or a missing folder link.
articles.summary: Common reasons a SharePoint folder or file does not open from BTPM and what to check next.
articles.body:
If a SharePoint folder or file does not open from BTPM, the most common reason is SharePoint permissions, not BTPM itself.

What to check

- Project access in BTPM is not the same as SharePoint file permission. Having access to the project in BTPM does not automatically grant access to the SharePoint folder.
- Confirm you are signed in to the correct Microsoft / SharePoint account in your browser. A personal or wrong tenant account can silently block the file.
- Open the link in a fresh browser tab. Cached sessions sometimes block SharePoint from opening.
- If the workspace library or project folder is not linked correctly, BTPM may show a warning on the Shared Files page or in the document section.

What to do next

- If you do not have SharePoint access, ask the SharePoint folder owner or your admin to grant access.
- If the BTPM link looks broken, ask a Project Manager or Org Admin to reconnect the project folder or confirm the workspace library is assigned.

What BTPM will not do

BTPM will not bypass SharePoint permissions. Document access is controlled by Microsoft / SharePoint.

articles.title: Power BI and BTPM KPI data
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Power BI is a future downstream reporting consumer of BTPM KPI data, not a write-back source.
articles.summary: Explains how Power BI should consume BTPM KPI Engine data in the future.
articles.body:
Power BI is planned as a future downstream reporting consumer for BTPM.

Current status:
Not yet implemented as a BTPM integration.

Important rule:
Power BI is not the transactional source for KPI submission.
Power BI should not write KPI values back into BTPM.
Power BI should not submit values to the external KPI App.
Power BI should not become a parallel KPI reporting truth.

The BTPM KPI Engine is the source for KPI reporting outputs.

Future Power BI reporting should consume:
- KPI definitions
- official KPI snapshots
- project context
- workspace context
- reporting indicators
- derived summary data where appropriate

Power BI should use BTPM data for monitoring and reporting.

It should not replace:
- Project KPI configuration
- manual KPI updates
- official KPI snapshots
- KPI App submission outbox
- BTPM permission logic
- BTPM audit and traceability

- Which projects have KPIs due?
- Which projects have overdue KPI snapshots?
- Which KPIs are not reportable?
- Which projects are improving or deteriorating?
- Which KPI snapshots were captured this period?
- Which KPIs are mapped to external reporting in the future?
- Which submissions succeeded or failed after KPI App integration is implemented?

Until Power BI integration is implemented, use BTPM's in-app dashboards and KPI views.

articles.title: KPI App integration
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The KPI App integration will send selected official BTPM KPI snapshots to the external KPI App through MuleSoft.
articles.summary: Explains the planned KPI App integration direction and what is not yet implemented.
articles.body:
The KPI App integration is planned as the next integration layer after the internal BTPM KPI Engine.

BTPM KPI Engine

KPI App mapping

Supabase protected backend / Edge Function layer
↓
MuleSoft KPI endpoint

External KPI App / MS SQL database

What BTPM will send

It should not recalculate project data separately.
It should not read directly from the dashboard.
It should not use Power BI as a write-back source.
It should not create a second manual reporting truth.

- BTPM workspace
- BTPM project
- BTPM KPI
- external KPI App KPI ID
- scenario ID
- currency ID
- reporting frequency

- active or inactive state

Carry-forward

If reporting is due but there is no current-period snapshot, a future mapping may allow BTPM to use the latest available official snapshot.

If carry-forward is used, the submission history must show that the submitted value was carried forward.

Daily rows

The KPI App may require daily-granularity rows.

Test connectivity

A test Edge Function has already proven that Supabase can call the MuleSoft test endpoint and write records into the KPI App test MS SQL database.

That test proves connectivity only.

- external KPI catalog
- BTPM-to-external mapping
- payload builder
- submission outbox
- retry handling
- Report Now
- scheduled reporting

articles.title: Should I use a risk or a blocker?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Use a risk for something that may happen later. Use a blocker for something already stopping progress now.
articles.summary: Risks and blockers should not be mixed. A risk is a possible future problem; a blocker is a current issue that is already preventing progress.
articles.body:
Use a risk when something may happen in the future and could affect the project.

Use a blocker when something is already stopping or materially delaying progress now.

A simple rule:

- If it might happen, record a risk.
- If it is already happening and work is stuck, record a blocker.

Examples:

- Risk: “Key users may not be available for UAT.”
- Blocker: “The test environment is unavailable, so UAT cannot start.”
- Risk: “Supplier confirmation may arrive late.”
- Blocker: “Supplier confirmation is already overdue and the next task cannot start.”

What to check before creating one:

1. Is the issue already stopping work?
2. Does someone need to actively remove it now?
3. Is it still uncertain, or has it already happened?
4. Who owns the next action?

Do not create everything as a blocker just to make it visible. If every concern becomes a blocker, the team loses the ability to separate future threats from current delivery problems.

articles.title: Are dependencies only visual?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: No. Dependencies should represent real sequencing logic, not only visual lines between tasks.
articles.summary: Dependencies are useful when one item must wait for another. They should help users understand timing, blockers, and schedule impact.
articles.body:
No. Dependencies should not be treated as only visual.

A dependency should represent real sequencing logic. It means one task, phase, or milestone depends on another before it can start, continue, or finish.

Examples:

- UAT cannot start until the test environment is ready.
- Training cannot be finalized until the process design is approved.
- Go-live cannot happen until critical defects are resolved.
- A report cannot be submitted until KPI values are updated.

Dependencies help users understand why work may be waiting and what may be affected if another item is delayed.

Do not add dependencies just to draw a nice timeline. If two tasks are related but one does not actually wait for the other, use a comment, description, or execution update instead.

Good dependency logic answers:

- What is waiting?
- What is it waiting for?
- What happens if the earlier item is late?
- Who owns the next action?

articles.title: Why can’t I edit something?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Editing depends on your role, workspace access, object state, and server-side permissions.
articles.summary: Short answer about edit restrictions.
articles.body:
If you cannot edit something, common reasons include:

- you do not have access to the project
- your project role is Viewer
- your project role is Contributor and the action requires Project Manager authority
- you have workspace access but not project access
- the item is archived or inactive
- the action is restricted to Workspace Admin or Org Admin
- the workflow intentionally requires editing from a different surface

BTPM now uses project-level access for project visibility and planning authority.

Workspace access alone does not guarantee visibility to every project in that workspace.

If you believe you should have access, contact your Workspace Admin or Org Admin.

articles.title: Project governance traceability
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Governance traceability helps teams show what reviews were expected, what happened, and what evidence was recorded.
articles.summary: Governance traceability connects review expectations with actual governance records and evidence. It helps teams prove that governance happened without turning BTPM into a meeting scheduler.
articles.body:
Project governance traceability helps a team show that the right governance happened at the right time.

In BTPM, governance is not only a meeting name. It should connect:

- what review was expected;
- who owned it;
- when it was expected;
- whether it happened;
- what evidence was recorded;
- what follow-up is needed.

This is useful for project reviews, steering committees, audits, and management reporting. It helps avoid relying only on memory, emails, or old meeting notes.

BTPM should not become the place where meetings are scheduled. Outlook and Teams still handle meeting invites and attendance. BTPM captures the governance expectation and the evidence that the review took place.

Good governance traceability answers:

- What review was expected?
- When was it due?
- Who owned it?
- Was it recorded?
- What evidence supports it?
- Are any governance actions overdue?

Keep governance lightweight. Record what is useful for delivery, accountability, and reporting. Do not turn governance into paperwork that nobody reads.

articles.title: How to set up a governance cadence
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Set up a governance cadence when a project needs a regular review rhythm and evidence expectation.
articles.summary: A governance cadence defines what review is expected, who owns it, how often it should happen, and what evidence should be recorded.
articles.body:
Set up a governance cadence when a project needs a regular review rhythm.

Examples include SteerCo, project team review, risk review, KPI review, sponsor check-in, vendor review, or phase gate review.

What to do:

1. Choose the governance event type.
2. Define the purpose of the review.
3. Assign an owner.
4. Set the frequency or next expected date.
5. Define what evidence should be recorded.
6. Keep the cadence active only while it is useful.
7. Review overdue or missing governance records during project reviews.

A good cadence is clear enough that the team knows what is expected. It should not be vague, such as “regular updates” without an owner or evidence expectation.

Do not create too many cadences. Governance should support project control, not create unnecessary administration.

BTPM does not schedule the meeting. Use Outlook or Teams for meeting invites. Use BTPM to define the expectation and record the evidence.

articles.title: How to record governance evidence
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Record governance evidence after a review happens so the project has a clear decision and follow-up trail.
articles.summary: Governance evidence should show what happened, what was decided, and what follow-up is needed. It should be useful, not bureaucratic.
articles.body:
Record governance evidence after a review, decision, or governance checkpoint happens.

The purpose is not to write a long meeting transcript. The purpose is to keep enough evidence so the team can understand what happened and what needs follow-up.

What to record:

1. The governance event or review type.
2. The date.
3. The main topic or decision.
4. Key evidence, such as notes, file, deck, or link.
5. Follow-up actions or open points.
6. Owner for follow-up where needed.

Good evidence is short, clear, and useful. For example:

“SteerCo completed. Sponsor approved revised go-live date. Updated status deck attached. Two follow-up actions assigned.”

Avoid vague records such as:

“Meeting done.”

If the review did not happen, do not create fake evidence. Update the governance status or next expected date honestly.

BTPM is the governance evidence record. Meeting invites, emails, or Teams notes can support the evidence, but they should not be the only place where governance history lives.

- Is each cadence owned?
- Are next expected dates correct?
- Are completed reviews recorded?
- Is evidence attached or described?

If a report looks wrong, first check the source governance data in BTPM. Then check reporting scope, sync timing, or Power BI filters.

Good governance reporting starts with good governance discipline in BTPM.

articles.tooltip_excerpt: Manual update history records changes over time. Official snapshots capture a controlled point-in-time KPI value.
articles.summary: KPI update history and official snapshots serve different purposes. History shows how values changed; snapshots preserve a controlled reporting value.
articles.body:
KPI update history and official snapshots are not the same thing.

KPI update history shows how a KPI value changed over time. It helps users understand the sequence of updates, comments, and reporting periods.

An official KPI snapshot captures a controlled point-in-time value. It is useful when the project needs a stable value for reporting, governance, or external submission.

Simple rule:

- Update history = how the KPI changed.
- Official snapshot = the value captured for a specific reporting purpose.

Use update history for normal tracking. Use snapshots when the value needs to be locked or referenced for a report, review, or integration process.

Do not rewrite history to make a report look better. If a KPI value was wrong, correct it through the proper update process and create a new snapshot if needed.

For KPI App-related reporting, the submitted or prepared value should come from the controlled KPI setup and the appropriate snapshot or approved reporting flow.

articles.tooltip_excerpt: Configure Project KPIs by defining what is measured, who owns it, how often it updates, and how it will be used in reporting.
articles.summary: Project KPIs should be configured before they are used in dashboards, snapshots, reports, or KPI App submissions.
articles.body:
Configure a Project KPI when the project needs a measurable indicator.

Before adding or changing a KPI, decide what the KPI is meant to show. A KPI should help the team understand performance, progress, risk, quality, value, or another measurable project outcome.

What to configure:

1. KPI name.
2. Description or measurement logic.
3. Owner or responsible person.
4. Target or expected direction.
5. Unit of measure.
6. Update frequency.
7. Reporting period where relevant.
8. Whether the KPI will be used in snapshots, dashboards, reports, or KPI App integration.

A good KPI is clear enough that another person understands how the value should be updated and interpreted.

Do not create KPIs just because a dashboard needs more numbers. If the measure does not help decision-making, it may not be a useful KPI.

If the KPI is connected to external reporting, make sure the definition and update process are stable before using it for submission.

articles.title: How to capture KPI snapshots
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Capture a KPI snapshot when a KPI value needs to be preserved for a specific reporting or governance point.
articles.summary: A KPI snapshot captures a controlled point-in-time value. Use snapshots when the value needs to be referenced later for reporting, governance, or integration.
articles.body:
Capture a KPI snapshot when a KPI value needs to be preserved for a specific point in time.

Snapshots are useful for:

- governance reviews;
- monthly or weekly reporting;
- KPI App reporting;
- management updates;
- phase gate evidence;
- comparing current values with previous periods.

Before capturing a snapshot, check:

1. Is the KPI definition clear?
2. Is the latest value correct?
3. Is the reporting period correct?
4. Is the owner or reviewer comfortable with the value?
5. Does the value need a comment or explanation?
6. Is the snapshot needed for a report or integration?

A snapshot is not the same as normal update history. Update history shows how values changed over time. A snapshot preserves a controlled value for a specific purpose.

Do not capture a snapshot just to hide incorrect history. If a value is wrong, correct it through the proper KPI update process, then capture a new snapshot if needed.

articles.title: Project-level access control
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Project access controls who can see or work on a project. Workspace access does not always mean full project access.
articles.summary: Project-level access helps protect project information and keep ownership clear. If a user cannot see or edit a project, access and role should be checked first.
articles.body:
Project-level access controls who can see or work on a specific project.

Workspace access and project access are related, but they are not always the same thing. A user may belong to a workspace but still need specific project access, depending on how the project is configured.

Common access levels may include:

- Viewer: can read project information.
- Contributor: can work on assigned or permitted items.
- Project Manager: can manage project planning and execution.
- Workspace Admin or Org Admin: can manage broader access and setup.

If someone cannot see a project, check:

1. Are they in the correct workspace?
2. Is the project active and not archived?
3. Do they have access to that specific project?
4. Are they using the correct account?
5. Does the project belong to the workspace they selected?

If someone can see a project but cannot edit it, check their project role. A viewer should not be able to edit project data.

BTPM Guide cannot grant access or bypass permissions. Access changes must be handled by an authorized user through the proper admin or project access process.

articles.title: How to manage project access
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Manage project access by confirming who needs visibility, who needs editing rights, and who should administer the project.
articles.summary: Project access should give people enough permission to do their work without exposing or changing more than necessary.
articles.body:
Project access controls who can see or work on a project.

Use project access management when someone needs to join a project, change role, or stop having access.

What to check:

1. What does the person need to do?
2. Do they only need to view the project?
3. Do they need to update tasks or project data?
4. Are they a project lead or administrator?
5. Do they also need SharePoint or Power BI access?
6. Should access be removed when their role ends?

Give the minimum access that lets the person do their work. Not every user needs admin rights.

If a user cannot see a project, check workspace, project access, account, and project status. If a user can see but cannot edit, check their role.

BTPM Guide cannot grant access, invite users, or change roles. An authorized Project Manager, Workspace Admin, Org Admin, or file/report owner must handle access changes through the proper process.

articles.title: Why can't I see a project?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Common reasons a project is not visible: no project access, wrong workspace, archived project, or workspace-only access.
articles.summary: Practical checks when a project does not appear in your project list.
articles.body:
If you cannot see a project you expect to see, the most common reasons are workspace context, project access, or project status.

What to check

- You are in the right workspace. Use the workspace selector at the top. If "All workspaces" or another workspace is selected, the project may be hidden.
- You have project access. Workspace access alone does not always grant project visibility. BTPM separates workspace access (entering the workspace) from project access (seeing a specific project).
- The project is active. Archived or inactive projects are hidden from normal project lists by design.
- The project actually belongs to this workspace. Projects do not move automatically between workspaces.

What to do next

- Switch workspace and try again.
- Ask a Project Manager, Workspace Admin, or Org Admin to confirm your project access and the project status.
- If access was recently changed, reload the page after the admin update.

What BTPM will not do

BTPM will not show projects you do not have access to, even if you know they exist in another workspace.

articles.tooltip_excerpt: Generated documents are outputs created from BTPM data, such as charters and status decks.
articles.summary: BTPM can generate useful documents from project and roadmap information. These outputs help with reporting and communication but do not replace the source data inside BTPM.
articles.body:
Generated documents are files created by BTPM from information already stored in the app. Examples include project charters, project status decks, and roadmap status decks.

These files are useful when you need to share a structured update outside the app, for example with a sponsor, steering committee, or wider project team. The document is an output. The source of truth remains in BTPM.

A generated document may use project details, phases, tasks, risks, blockers, KPIs, governance information, or roadmap filters depending on the document type. After generation, the file can be stored or linked through the relevant file/output area.

Use generated documents when you need a clear snapshot for communication. Keep BTPM updated first, then generate the document. If the project data changes later, generate a fresh version rather than manually editing an old output and treating it as the source.

Generated documents do not create or change project records by themselves. They reflect the information available at the time they are generated.

articles.title: How to refresh a Project Charter

articles.summary: The Project Charter is a structured project document generated from BTPM. Refresh it after meaningful project setup or scope changes, then share the latest version with stakeholders.
articles.body:
Use the Project Charter when you need a clean project summary for sponsors, governance reviews, or project onboarding.

Before refreshing the charter, check that the Project Overview is up to date. Pay special attention to the project description, goals, scope, dates, owner, team, risks, KPIs, and governance information.

To refresh the charter:

1. Open the project.
2. Go to the Project Overview.
3. Review the main project information.
4. Use the charter generation or refresh action available on the page.
5. Wait for BTPM to create the document.
6. Open the generated file or linked output once it is ready.

The charter is a snapshot. If you later update the project in BTPM, the old charter does not automatically become current. Generate a new version when you need an updated document.

Do not use the charter as the place to manually maintain project truth. Keep the project data in BTPM updated first, then refresh the charter.

The Weekly Project Status Deck is a generated presentation-style output for project updates. It is intended for weekly reviews, sponsor updates, project team meetings, or steering discussions where a clear project snapshot is needed.

The deck should reflect the information available in BTPM at the time it is generated. Depending on the project setup, it may include project status, dates, phases, tasks, risks, blockers, KPIs, governance information, and recent updates.

Use it when you need to communicate status outside the app. Before generating the deck, check that the project information is current. If the project has stale tasks, missing KPI updates, or unresolved blocker information, the deck will reflect that.

The deck is not a separate planning tool. Do not maintain status manually in the PowerPoint and then expect BTPM to follow it. Update BTPM first, then generate the deck.

articles.summary: BTPM can prepare governed reporting data for Power BI. BTPM remains the source of truth; Power BI is used for reporting and analysis.
articles.body:
Power BI is used as a reporting layer for BTPM. It helps teams build dashboards and management reports from governed BTPM data.

The important rule is simple: BTPM remains the source of truth. Project records, phases, tasks, risks, blockers, KPIs, governance data, and access rules are maintained in BTPM. Power BI consumes prepared reporting data from BTPM; it should not become a separate place where project truth is manually maintained.

Admins can use the Power BI area to validate the connection, manage the reporting bridge, trigger or review sync behavior where available, and check whether reporting data is fresh enough for use.

Use Power BI when you need broader reporting, executive dashboards, or analysis across projects and workspaces. Use BTPM when you need to update the actual project data.

articles.title: Using the Power BI Admin page

articles.summary: Power BI Admin is the Org Admin surface for managing BTPM's governed downstream Power BI reporting connection. BTPM remains the source of truth; Power BI is a reporting layer.
articles.body:
The Power BI Admin page is for Org Admins who manage BTPM's governed downstream reporting connection to Power BI.

Use this page to configure or validate the connection, refresh permission cache, provision the BTPM Bridge semantic model, control outbound data scope, run a manual sync, and review sync observability or Bridge QA where available.

Main operational areas:

1. Connection and validation. Use this area to check connection status, validate configuration, refresh permission cache, and provision or reset/re-provision the BTPM Bridge model where needed.

2. Data scope. Use this area to control which organizations, workspaces, projects, or reporting scopes are included in outbound Power BI data.

3. Manual sync. Use manual sync when an Org Admin wants to push the governed BTPM reporting data to Power BI on demand.

4. Sync observability and Bridge QA. Use these sections to check sync status, row counts, warnings, failed stages, and whether the bridge data looks ready for reporting.

Important boundaries:
- Power BI is downstream reporting; BTPM remains the source of truth.
- Power BI should not become a separate manual project-management source.
- Refreshing/syncing Power BI does not change live BTPM project records.
- Power BI access and Microsoft workspace permissions may still need to be managed outside BTPM.
- Guide Mode can explain the Power BI Admin surfaces but must not run sync, provision, reset, or grant Power BI access on behalf of the user.
- Developer diagnostics should not be presented as normal workflow guidance unless the user explicitly asks about admin troubleshooting.

The KPI App integration helps BTPM connect KPI reporting with an external KPI process.

In BTPM, KPIs are defined, owned, updated, and tracked with history. Some KPIs may also be mapped to the KPI App so they can be prepared or submitted through the agreed integration process.

The key idea is control. BTPM should not send random dashboard numbers. KPI App reporting should use the proper BTPM KPI setup, mapping, reporting period, and official snapshot or approved value flow.

For normal users, the important part is to keep KPI definitions and updates accurate in BTPM. For admins, the KPI App area is where mappings, catalog checks, reporting readiness, and submission status can be managed.
