articles.title: Using the KPI App Admin page
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Use KPI App Integration to manage mappings, readiness, reporting actions, submission monitoring, scheduling, and protocol status.
articles.summary: The KPI App Admin page is the operational admin surface for connecting BTPM KPI data to the external KPI App process through governed mappings, outbox records, submission monitoring, scheduling, and protocol controls.
articles.body:
The KPI App Integration page is for Org Admins who manage how BTPM KPI data connects to the external KPI App process.

Use this page for real operational admin work such as mapping BTPM KPIs to external KPI definitions, checking readiness, running Report Now, monitoring submissions, retrying or resetting failed submissions, and reviewing scheduling or protocol status.

Main operational areas:

1. Mappings. Use mappings to connect BTPM KPI definitions to external KPI App identifiers and submission rules. Creating or editing a mapping prepares the integration; it does not itself submit data.

2. Report Now. Use Report Now when an authorized admin needs to prepare and submit a KPI App payload manually for a known reporting period and validity date.

3. Submission Monitor. Use the monitor to review outbox/submission state, submitted periods, HTTP/submission status, errors, and retry/reset options where available.

4. Retry and Reset. Retry is used when an existing submission attempt should be tried again. Reset is used when a mapping or outbox state needs to be cleared for a new controlled Report Now flow.

5. Scheduling and protocol. Scheduling and automation protocol sections help admins understand scheduled submission readiness, protocol state, and automation status. These are governed admin surfaces, not AI actions.

Important boundaries:
- BTPM does not automatically approve KPI submissions as an AI action.
- Report Now must follow the configured outbox/protocol flow.
- Guide Mode can explain the KPI App admin surfaces but must not submit, retry, reset, approve, or bypass the protocol on behalf of a user.
- Developer/test-only surfaces, API read tests, values-readback placeholders, and diagnostic test runners are not normal user workflows and should not be presented as standard Admin guidance.

question_examples: What is the KPI App Integration page for?
How do KPI App mappings work?
What does Report Now do?
Where do I check KPI App submission status?
When should I retry or reset a KPI App submission?
Can BTPM automatically approve KPI submissions?
answer_rules: Use this article for broad KPI App Admin questions.
For exact manual submission steps, use workflow-kpi-app-report-now.
Explain that mappings prepare the integration but do not submit by themselves.
Explain outbox/protocol/submission monitor at a high level.
Do not present developer/test diagnostics as normal user workflows.
forbidden_claims: Do not say BTPM Guide can submit, retry, reset, approve, or bypass protocol.
Do not say KPI App submission is automatic AI approval.
Do not present KPI API read test or values readback placeholder as normal operational guidance.
Do not use KPI App guidance for workspace creation, project creation, or Admin Users questions.

articles.title: KPI Automation Protocol
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The KPI Automation Protocol helps admins review the controlled KPI integration process and submission status.
articles.summary: The KPI Automation Protocol gives admins a structured view of KPI integration readiness, reporting periods, payload status, and submission monitoring.
articles.body:
The KPI Automation Protocol is an admin-facing view of the controlled KPI reporting process.

It helps admins understand which KPI mappings are active, which reporting period is being handled, whether a KPI payload is ready, and what happened during submission. It is useful when you need to review integration status, investigate why a report is not ready, or confirm what was submitted.

Use the protocol as an evidence and monitoring aid. It should help answer questions such as:

- Which KPI was mapped?
- Which period was reported?
- Was the payload ready?
- Was it submitted?
- Did the latest attempt succeed or fail?

The protocol does not replace the KPI definition or KPI update history in the project. It is a reporting and integration trace view. If KPI values are wrong, fix the source KPI setup and history in BTPM, then use the integration process again.

question_examples: What is the KPI Automation Protocol?
What does the KPI protocol show?
Does the protocol replace KPI history?
answer_rules: Explain the protocol as admin evidence/monitoring.
State that KPI definitions and history remain the source.
Keep answer practical.
forbidden_claims: The protocol replaces KPI definitions.
The protocol is where users manually maintain KPI values.

articles.title: SharePoint output behavior
articles.tooltip_excerpt: SharePoint can store or link BTPM outputs, but BTPM remains the place where project data is maintained.
articles.summary: BTPM can connect project files and generated outputs with SharePoint. SharePoint is used for document storage and access, while BTPM keeps the project structure and source data.
articles.body:
SharePoint is used with BTPM to store, link, or access project-related documents and generated outputs.

A generated file, such as a charter or status deck, may be saved or linked through the project file/output area depending on the configured setup. Uploaded or linked project files may also be visible from the relevant file surfaces.

The important distinction is this: SharePoint stores documents; BTPM manages the project data. If a project status, task, risk, blocker, KPI, or governance record changes, update it in BTPM first. Then generate or refresh the document output if needed.

If a file is missing, first check whether the project has the correct SharePoint folder or connection. If you cannot access a file, it may be a permissions or setup issue, not a project data issue.

question_examples: Where do generated files go?
What is SharePoint used for in BTPM?
Why can't I see a generated file?
answer_rules: Explain that SharePoint stores documents and BTPM manages project data.
Mention folder/connection/permission checks for missing files.
Do not imply that SharePoint edits update BTPM project fields.
forbidden_claims: SharePoint is the source of truth for BTPM project data.
Editing a PowerPoint in SharePoint updates BTPM.

articles.title: Using My Work
articles.tooltip_excerpt: My Work shows the items that need your attention, such as assigned tasks, due work, and upcoming actions.
articles.summary: Use My Work as your personal action view in BTPM. It helps you focus on work assigned to you, upcoming deadlines, overdue items, and items that may need an update.
articles.body:
My Work is your personal action page in BTPM. Use it when you want to understand what needs your attention without opening every project one by one.

This page helps you focus on items connected to you, such as assigned tasks, upcoming due dates, overdue work, and items that may require progress updates. It is useful at the start of the day or before a project review.

What to do here:

1. Check what is due or overdue.
2. Open the relevant task, phase, project, or item.
3. Update the status, progress, or execution note where needed.
4. Review upcoming items so you can act before they become late.
5. Use filters if the page shows more work than you need right now.

My Work is not a full project planning page. If you need to change project structure, dates, dependencies, or ownership, open the relevant project page.

A good habit is to use My Work as your daily starting point, then use the project pages for deeper planning and review.

question_examples: What do I do on My Work?
Why should I use My Work?
Where do I see tasks assigned to me?
How do I know what needs my attention?
answer_rules: Explain My Work as a personal action view.
Tell users to open project pages for deeper planning changes.
Keep the answer focused on daily use.
forbidden_claims: My Work replaces project planning.
My Work shows every project item regardless of assignment or access.

articles.title: Using the Projects page
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Projects page helps you find, open, filter, and review projects in your selected workspace.
articles.summary: Use the Projects page to browse projects, check high-level status, and open the project you need to work on. It is the entry point into project execution.
articles.body:
The Projects page is where you find and open projects in the selected workspace.

Use this page when you want to see which projects exist, check their high-level status, or quickly move into a specific project. Depending on your access, you may also be able to create or manage projects from here.

What to do here:

1. Confirm you are in the right workspace.
2. Use filters or search to find the project you need.
3. Review high-level project signals such as status, health, owner, or dates.
4. Open the project to work with its overview, planning, KPIs, risks, governance, files, or Gantt.
5. If you cannot see a project, check whether you are in the correct workspace or whether you have access.

The Projects page is not where detailed project work is maintained. It helps you find and enter the right project. Detailed updates happen inside the project itself.

question_examples: What do I do on the Projects page?
Why can't I see a project?
Where do I open a project?
Is this where I update project details?
answer_rules: Explain that the page is for finding and opening projects.
Mention workspace context and access if a project is missing.
Direct users to project detail pages for actual updates.
forbidden_claims: The Projects page is where all project details are edited.
Users can see every project regardless of workspace access.

articles.title: Using the Project Overview
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Project Overview is the main summary page for project purpose, scope, status, ownership, and key signals.
articles.summary: Use the Project Overview to understand the project quickly and keep its main information clear for stakeholders. It is the front page of the project.
articles.body:
The Project Overview is the project's front page. It should help a user understand what the project is, why it matters, who owns it, and what the current situation is.

Use this page to review or maintain the main project information, such as description, goals, scope, dates, status, owner, team, key risks, KPIs, and governance signals.

What to do here:

1. Check whether the project summary still explains the work clearly.
2. Review status, health, dates, and ownership.
3. Keep scope and goals understandable for someone outside the core team.
4. Use linked sections to move into planning, KPIs, risks, governance, files, or Gantt when you need detail.
5. Generate or refresh project outputs, such as a charter or status deck, only after the underlying project data is updated.

The Project Overview should not become a dumping ground. Keep it concise. Detailed task updates, KPI history, risks, blockers, and governance evidence belong in their dedicated pages.

question_examples: What do I do on the Project Overview?
What should I update before generating a charter?
Where should I put project goals and scope?
Is this where I update task progress?
answer_rules: Explain the overview as the project front page.
Tell users to keep it concise and use dedicated pages for detail.
Mention generated outputs only as downstream outputs after source data is updated.
forbidden_claims: The overview replaces task, KPI, risk, and governance pages.
Generated decks or charters are the source of truth.

articles.title: Using the Project Planning page
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Project Planning page is where you structure the project into phases, tasks, owners, dates, and dependencies.
articles.summary: Use Project Planning to break a project into executable work. This is where phases and tasks become clear enough for people to own and update.
articles.body:
The Project Planning page is where the project becomes an executable plan.

Use it to organize the project into phases and tasks, assign ownership, set dates, and make the work clear enough for the team to execute. A good plan helps users understand what has to happen, who owns it, and when it is expected.

What to do here:

1. Review the project phases.
2. Add or update tasks under the correct phase.
3. Set owners, due dates, status, priority, and other planning fields where available.
4. Keep task names action-oriented and specific.
5. Use dependencies carefully when one item must wait for another.
6. Move into task or phase details when you need deeper execution updates.

Project Planning is not a free-form notes area. Use comments and execution updates for discussion and progress history. Use the Gantt if you need timeline visibility or controlled date movement.

question_examples: What do I do on the Project Planning page?
How should I plan phases and tasks?
Where do I add tasks?
Should I use comments for planning?
answer_rules: Explain that planning structures work into phases and tasks.
Tell users to use execution updates/comments for progress and discussion.
Mention Gantt as timeline visibility, not a separate planning truth.
forbidden_claims: Planning should be maintained separately from BTPM.
Comments are the main source of task planning.

articles.title: Using the Phase detail page
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Phase detail page helps you review one phase, its tasks, progress, ownership, and execution updates.
articles.summary: Use the Phase detail page when you need to focus on one stage of the project and understand whether that stage is moving as expected.
articles.body:
The Phase detail page focuses on one phase of a project. A phase is a major stage of delivery, such as Design, Build, UAT, Training, or Go-Live.

Use this page to understand what the phase is meant to achieve, which tasks belong to it, who is responsible, and whether progress is on track.

What to do here:

1. Review the phase purpose, status, dates, and owner.
2. Check the tasks inside the phase.
3. Look for overdue work, blockers, risks, or unclear ownership.
4. Add a dated execution update when there is meaningful progress or a status change.
5. Use comments for discussion or context that does not need to become a formal progress update.
6. Open individual tasks for detailed task-level work.

The Phase detail page helps you manage a project stage. It should not replace task-level updates where the actual work happens.

question_examples: What do I do on a Phase detail page?
What is a phase in BTPM?
Should I update the phase or the task?
When should I add a phase execution update?
answer_rules: Explain phase as a major project stage.
Distinguish phase-level review from task-level execution.
Explain comments versus execution updates briefly.
forbidden_claims: A phase replaces task-level execution.
Comments and execution updates are the same thing.

articles.title: Using the Task detail page
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Task detail page is where a specific work item is updated, discussed, and tracked.
articles.summary: Use the Task detail page for the real execution of one work item: status, owner, due date, progress notes, comments, blockers, and related context.
articles.body:
The Task detail page is where you work with one specific task.

A task is the executable work item inside a phase. It should be specific enough that someone can own it, update it, and know when it is done.

What to do here:

1. Check the task title, owner, priority, status, and due date.
2. Update the task when progress changes.
3. Add a dated execution update when you need to record meaningful progress.
4. Use comments for discussion, clarification, or context.
5. Review blockers, risks, dependencies, or linked files if they are connected to the task.
6. Mark the task complete only when the work is actually done.

Keep task updates clear and useful. Avoid vague updates like "working on it" if the team needs real progress information. A better update explains what changed, what is next, and whether anything is blocking the task.

question_examples: What do I do on a Task detail page?
When should I add an execution update?
What is the difference between a comment and a task update?
How should I update task progress?
answer_rules: Explain task as executable work.
Encourage specific progress updates.
Distinguish comments from execution updates.
forbidden_claims: Task comments are the official progress history.
A task should be closed before the work is done.

articles.title: Using the Project Gantt
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Project Gantt shows project timing from the same phases and tasks used in BTPM planning.
articles.summary: Use the Gantt to see the project timeline, sequence work, and understand timing. It should reflect BTPM planning data, not create a separate plan.
articles.body:
The Project Gantt is the timeline view of your project. It helps you see when phases and tasks are planned, how work is sequenced, and where timing may need attention.

Use the Gantt when you need to understand the project schedule visually. It is especially useful for spotting overlapping work, long phases, tight timelines, or date changes that may affect delivery.

What to do here:

1. Review phases and tasks on the timeline.
2. Check whether dates look realistic.
3. Look for overdue or high-risk areas.
4. Use edit mode only if you have permission and need to adjust dates.
5. Confirm that schedule changes still make sense with dependencies and project commitments.

The Gantt is not a separate planning database. It should show and update the same canonical project dates used elsewhere in BTPM. Do not maintain one plan in the Gantt and a different plan in the task list.

question_examples: What do I do on the Gantt page?
Is the Gantt a separate plan?
When should I use Gantt edit mode?
How do date changes affect the project?
answer_rules: Explain Gantt as timeline view of existing BTPM planning data.
State it is not a separate planning truth.
Mention edit mode only for authorized users.
forbidden_claims: Gantt stores a separate project plan.
Users should maintain one plan in Gantt and another in task planning.

articles.title: Using Project KPIs
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Project KPIs help you track measurable outcomes, targets, updates, and official snapshots.
articles.summary: Use Project KPIs to define what should be measured, update values over time, and support reliable reporting through KPI history and snapshots.
articles.body:
The Project KPIs page is where measurable project indicators are managed.

Use KPIs when you need more than a status comment. A good KPI has a clear name, target, owner, frequency, and update history. It should help the team understand whether the project is achieving something measurable.

What to do here:

1. Review existing KPI definitions.
2. Check whether targets, owners, and update frequency are clear.
3. Add or update KPI values when new information is available.
4. Review KPI history before using the number in reporting.
5. Capture or use an official snapshot where that is part of the process.
6. For KPI App-connected KPIs, make sure mapping and reporting readiness are handled through the admin process.

Do not use KPI fields for general comments. If something cannot be measured meaningfully, it may belong in a project update, risk, blocker, or governance note instead.

question_examples: What do I do on the Project KPIs page?
How should I update a KPI?
What is KPI history used for?
Should I use a KPI for general comments?
answer_rules: Explain KPIs as measurable indicators with history.
Mention official snapshots where relevant.
Keep KPI App integration separate from normal project KPI updates.
forbidden_claims: KPI fields should be used for general comments.
KPI App mappings are managed by every normal user from the project page.

articles.title: Using Risks and Blockers
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Use Risks and Blockers to separate future threats from current issues that are already stopping progress.
articles.summary: The Risks and Blockers page helps teams track what might go wrong and what is already preventing progress. Keeping them separate makes project reviews clearer.
articles.body:
The Risks and Blockers page is where you manage two different kinds of project concerns.

A risk is something that may happen in the future and could affect the project. A blocker is a current issue that is already preventing progress.

What to do here:

1. Add a risk when there is a future threat that needs monitoring or mitigation.
2. Add a blocker when work is currently stuck.
3. Assign an owner so the item is not just recorded but actively managed.
4. Keep impact, priority, mitigation, and next steps clear.
5. Update or resolve items when the situation changes.
6. Use the page during project reviews to focus attention on what needs action.

Do not mix risks and blockers into one general issue list. If everything becomes a blocker, the team loses the ability to separate future concern from immediate obstruction.

question_examples: What do I do on the Risks and Blockers page?
What is the difference between a risk and a blocker?
When should I create a blocker?
How should I manage mitigation?
answer_rules: Clearly distinguish risk from blocker.
Tell users to assign owners and update/resolve items.
Avoid merging risks and blockers into one generic issue concept.
forbidden_claims: Risks and blockers are the same thing.
Every concern should be recorded as a blocker.

articles.title: Using Project Governance
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Project Governance helps you define expected reviews and record evidence that governance happened.
articles.summary: Use Project Governance to manage review cadence, governance records, and evidence. BTPM does not schedule meetings; it helps you track what governance is expected and what was recorded.
articles.body:
The Project Governance page helps you manage project review expectations and evidence.

Use this page to define governance cadence, such as regular SteerCo, project team review, risk review, KPI review, or sponsor check-in. A cadence tells the team what review is expected, who owns it, when the next one is due, and what evidence should be recorded.

What to do here:

1. Review active governance cadences.
2. Check the next expected date and owner.
3. Record a governance event after the review happens.
4. Attach or describe the evidence where required.
5. Follow up on overdue or missing governance records.
6. Keep governance practical and lightweight.

BTPM does not create the calendar meeting or manage attendees. Outlook or Teams should still handle scheduling. BTPM captures the expectation and the evidence.

question_examples: What do I do on the Governance page?
What is governance cadence?
Does BTPM schedule meetings?
How do I record governance evidence?
answer_rules: Explain governance cadence and records in practical terms.
State clearly that BTPM does not schedule meetings.
Keep the answer focused on evidence and review discipline.
forbidden_claims: BTPM sends calendar invitations.
Governance cadence is the meeting itself.

articles.title: Using the Roadmap
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Roadmap shows cross-project status, filters, timeline, dashboard, calendar, and reporting views.
articles.summary: Use the Roadmap to review work across projects, programs, and workspaces. It helps you understand portfolio status without opening every project.
articles.body:
The Roadmap is the cross-project view in BTPM. Use it when you need to understand status across multiple projects, programs, or workspaces.

The Roadmap can help you review progress, health, dates, stages, overdue work, active risks, blockers, and reporting outputs depending on the view you select.

What to do here:

1. Confirm the selected workspace or workspaces.
2. Use filters for programs, projects, status, health, or other available criteria.
3. Review the Overview or Dashboard for high-level signals.
4. Use Timeline when timing and sequencing matter.
5. Use Calendar when dates and upcoming milestones matter.
6. Generate a Roadmap Status Deck only after the filters show the scope you want to report.

The Roadmap is a reporting and navigation surface. It should derive from project data, not become a separate place to maintain project truth.

question_examples: What do I do on the Roadmap?
How should I use Roadmap filters?
What is the difference between Overview, Dashboard, Timeline, and Calendar?
When should I generate a Roadmap Status Deck?
answer_rules: Explain Roadmap as a cross-project reporting/navigation view.
Tell users to check filters before generating deck outputs.
State that Roadmap derives from project data.
forbidden_claims: Roadmap is a separate project data source.
Updating the Roadmap directly replaces updating project records.

articles.title: Agile mode in BTPM
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Agile mode adds backlog, sprint, and board views for projects that need a lighter iterative planning style.
articles.summary: Agile mode helps teams manage work through backlog items, sprints, and a board while keeping the normal BTPM project structure intact.

question_examples: What is Agile mode in BTPM?
Does Agile mode replace phases and tasks?
When should I use backlog and sprints?
answer_rules: Explain Agile mode as optional and additive.
State that it does not replace the normal BTPM project structure.
Avoid generic Scrum theory.
forbidden_claims: Agile mode replaces phases, tasks, governance, or KPIs.
Every project should use Agile mode.

articles.title: Using the Agile Backlog
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Agile Backlog is where you collect, clarify, and prioritize work before moving it into sprints or execution.
articles.summary: Use the Agile Backlog to keep future work visible and ordered. It helps the team decide what should be worked on next.
articles.body:
The Agile Backlog is the list of work that may need to be done but is not necessarily being worked on right now.

Use it to collect ideas, requests, improvements, fixes, or work items that need prioritization. A good backlog helps the team avoid losing important work while still keeping active execution focused.

What to do here:

1. Add work items that may need to be done.
2. Keep titles clear and action-oriented.
3. Clarify the description enough so the team understands the expected outcome.
4. Prioritize the most important items near the top.
5. Move items into a sprint when the team is ready to work on them.
6. Remove, archive, or deprioritize items that are no longer relevant.

The backlog is not a dumping ground. If every idea stays forever and nothing is prioritized, the backlog stops helping. Keep it clean and useful.

question_examples: What do I do in the Agile Backlog?
How should I prioritize backlog items?
Is the backlog a dumping ground?
answer_rules: Explain backlog as future/prioritized work.
Tell users to keep it clean and actionable.
Explain when items should move into a sprint.
forbidden_claims: The backlog is where all project records should be stored.
Backlog items replace every task in all projects.

articles.title: Using Sprints in BTPM
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Sprints are short delivery periods that help an agile-enabled project focus on selected work.
articles.summary: Use sprints to group selected backlog items into a clear delivery window. They help the team focus and review progress regularly.
articles.body:
A sprint is a short delivery period for selected work. It helps the team focus on what should be completed next instead of trying to work on everything at once.

Use sprints when a project is agile-enabled and the team wants a regular rhythm for planning, execution, and review.

What to do here:

1. Create or open the relevant sprint.
2. Set a clear sprint goal if the page supports it.
3. Add the backlog items or work items the team agrees to focus on.
4. Check that the sprint dates are realistic.
5. Review progress during the sprint.
6. Close or complete the sprint when the cycle ends, then decide what happens to unfinished work.

A sprint is not the same as a project phase. A phase is a major delivery stage. A sprint is a short timebox used by agile teams to focus execution.

question_examples: What is a sprint in BTPM?
What do I do on the Sprints page?
Is a sprint the same as a phase?
answer_rules: Explain sprint as a short delivery period.
Distinguish sprint from phase.
Keep the guidance business-friendly and not Scrum-heavy.
forbidden_claims: Sprint and phase mean the same thing.
Sprints replace project governance.

articles.title: Using the Agile Board
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Agile Board shows selected work by workflow state so the team can see what is planned, active, and done.
articles.summary: Use the Agile Board to manage day-to-day movement of agile work. It helps the team see flow, progress, and items that may be stuck.
articles.body:
The Agile Board is a visual execution view for agile-enabled projects.

It shows work by workflow state, such as planned, in progress, blocked, review, or done depending on the project setup. The board helps the team understand what is moving, what is waiting, and what needs attention.

What to do here:

1. Review the columns or workflow states.
2. Check which items are active.
3. Move items only when their real status changes.
4. Look for work that is stuck too long.
5. Keep item titles and owners clear.
6. Use comments or execution updates when more context is needed.

The board is not a separate truth. Moving an item on the board should reflect the real work status. Do not use the board only for appearance while the actual project plan says something different.

question_examples: What do I do on the Agile Board?
When should I move an item on the board?
Is the board a separate project plan?
answer_rules: Explain board as visual execution view.
State that board movement should reflect real status.
Reinforce that the board is not a separate truth.
forbidden_claims: The board is independent from BTPM project data.
Moving cards is only cosmetic.

articles.title: Project Templates
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Project Templates help teams reuse a proven project structure instead of creating every project from scratch.
articles.summary: Use Project Templates when similar projects repeat. Templates help standardize phases, tasks, and setup while still allowing each project to be adjusted.

question_examples: What are Project Templates?
When should I use a template?
Is a template the final project plan?
answer_rules: Explain templates as reusable starting structures.
Tell users to adjust the generated project after creation.
Warn against overloaded templates.
forbidden_claims: A template is always the final project plan.
Templates should include every possible task just in case.

articles.title: Project Baseline vs current plan
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The baseline is the agreed reference point. The current plan is the working plan the team updates during execution.
articles.summary: A project baseline should help compare approved expectations with the current working plan. Do not invent or silently change approved baseline dates without a clear governance reason.
articles.body:
A project baseline is the agreed reference point for the project plan.

The current plan is the working version the team uses during execution.

Use the baseline to understand what was originally approved or committed. Use the current plan to manage what the team is working with now.

If dates change after a baseline was approved, do not silently rewrite the baseline just to make the project look on track.

First clarify what changed:

1. Did only the current delivery plan change?
2. Was there a formal decision to change the approved baseline?
3. Is there governance evidence for the change?
4. Should the change be reflected as a current-plan update, a new approved baseline, or a governance record?
5. Who is authorized to approve the change?

BTPM Guide cannot change baseline dates for you.

Verified baseline actions in BTPM (Project Overview — Baseline section):

- Approve baseline: freezes the current dates as the approved baseline (only available before a baseline exists, after the preflight shows 'Ready to baseline').
- Rebaseline: OVERWRITES the existing approved baseline with the current planned dates after a confirmation preflight. The previous baseline is not recoverable. The action is logged in Baseline history.

What is NOT supported in BTPM:

- There is no Baseline Settings page and no per-date baseline editor.
- You cannot edit an approved baseline date in place.
- You cannot create a new baseline alongside an existing approved baseline. Rebaseline overwrites.
- The Gantt and Project Planning pages do not edit the baseline. Editing current planned dates there does not change the approved baseline values.

If approved dates need to change: update the current plan through the normal planning process, record the governance reason/evidence, and only use Rebaseline on the Project Overview if your organization has formally decided to replace the approved baseline.

The baseline should preserve accountability. The current plan should reflect today's execution reality.

question_examples: How can I change baseline dates if they are already approved?
Can I edit an approved baseline?
What is the difference between baseline and current plan?
Should I create a new baseline if dates change?
Can BTPM Guide change the baseline for me?
answer_rules: Do not invent baseline settings or baseline edit controls.
Explain baseline as approved reference and current plan as working plan.
Say approved baseline changes need governance reason/evidence.
If exact UI is not verified, say exact click-by-click baseline change steps are not available.
State that BTPM Guide cannot change baseline dates.
forbidden_claims: BTPM Guide can change baseline dates.
Users should silently rewrite approved baseline dates.
There is a Baseline Settings page.
Users can create a new baseline from an approved baseline.
Editing Gantt automatically changes the approved baseline.

articles.title: Project lifecycle, status, stage, and health
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Lifecycle, status, stage, and health answer different questions about a project and should not be mixed.
articles.summary: BTPM uses different project signals for different purposes. Status, stage, health, progress, and lifecycle are related, but they are not the same thing.
articles.body:
BTPM uses several signals to describe a project. They should not be mixed.

Lifecycle tells whether the project is active, paused, completed, archived, or otherwise in a major lifecycle state.

Stage tells where the project is in its delivery journey, such as initiation, planning, execution, testing, or closure.

Status tells the workflow position of the work, such as planned, in progress, completed, or blocked, depending on the object.

Health tells whether the project looks okay, at risk, or off track.

Progress tells how much of the work is complete.

Simple rule:

- Stage = where we are in the journey.
- Status = what is happening with the work.
- Health = whether the situation looks safe.
- Progress = how much is done.
- Lifecycle = whether the project is active, paused, completed, or archived.

Do not use one field to explain everything. Clear signals make reporting and decision-making easier.

question_examples: What is the difference between status and health?
What is project stage?
What does lifecycle mean?
Why does BTPM have several project signals?
answer_rules: Explain each signal in simple terms.
Make clear they answer different questions.
Avoid technical implementation terms.
forbidden_claims: Status, health, progress, and stage are the same thing.
One field should be used to explain everything.

articles.title: Saved views and filters
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Filters and saved views help you focus reporting on the right workspace, program, project, or status scope.
articles.summary: Use filters to narrow what you see. Use saved views when you regularly need the same reporting scope or roadmap setup.
articles.body:
Filters help you focus on the information you need. Saved views help you return to a useful filter setup later.

In BTPM, filters may help you narrow a page by workspace, program, project, status, health, owner, date, or other available criteria depending on the page.

Use filters when the page shows too much information. For example, on the Roadmap you may want to show only one program, selected projects, at-risk work, or a specific workspace scope.

Use a saved view when the same filter setup is useful repeatedly, such as a management view, team view, steering committee view, or personal follow-up view.

Before generating a report or deck, always check the active filters. The output should reflect the scope you intended to show.

question_examples: How should I use filters?
What are saved views?
Why should I check filters before generating a deck?
answer_rules: Explain filters as a way to narrow scope.
Explain saved views as reusable filter setups.
Remind users to check filters before reports/decks.
forbidden_claims: Saved views create separate project data.
Filters change the underlying project records.

articles.title: Project Team and RACI
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Project Team and RACI area helps clarify who is involved and what role they play in project delivery.
articles.summary: Use Project Team and RACI to show who is responsible, accountable, consulted, or informed for important project work.
articles.body:
The Project Team and RACI area helps clarify who is involved in a project and how they contribute.

RACI is a simple way to describe responsibility:

- Responsible: does the work.
- Accountable: owns the outcome.
- Consulted: gives input before decisions or actions.
- Informed: needs to be kept updated.

Use this area when unclear ownership is slowing work down or when the project needs visible accountability across functions.

What to do here:

1. Review who is part of the project team.
2. Assign roles where ownership needs to be clear.
3. Use RACI for important project or phase responsibilities.
4. Keep task execution simple; not every small task needs a full RACI setup.
5. Update the team when people join, leave, or change role.

RACI should help the team work more clearly. It should not become an administrative burden that makes simple work harder.

question_examples: What is RACI?
What do I do on the Project Team page?
Should every task have RACI?
What is the difference between responsible and accountable?
answer_rules: Explain RACI in simple terms.
State that RACI should clarify ownership, not add bureaucracy.
Mention that simple task execution does not always need full RACI.
forbidden_claims: Every task must have full RACI.
RACI replaces task assignments.

articles.title: Why can't I edit a project or task?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Edit rights depend on your project role, project status, and admin overrides. Viewers and read-only roles cannot change content.
articles.summary: Practical reasons editing is blocked on a project or task, and what to check next.
articles.body:
If you cannot edit a project or task, the cause is usually your role, the project status, or admin configuration.

What to check

- Your project role. Viewers can read but cannot edit. Contributors can edit assigned work. Project Managers can manage planning and execution. Org and Workspace Admins have override authority at their level.
- The project status. Projects in a closed, archived, or read-only state are intentionally restricted from edits.
- Task ownership and assignment. Some fields only the assignee, owner, or Project Manager can change.
- Whether the item is part of a baseline or locked planning view. Locked items are read-only on purpose.

What to do next

- Ask the Project Manager or an Org Admin to confirm your role on this project.
- Ask the Project Manager to reopen the project or item if it was closed in error.
- If the field is governed (status, stage, lifecycle), use the proper action rather than trying to edit it directly.

What BTPM will not do

BTPM will not silently let you edit projects or tasks you do not have rights on. Permissions are enforced on the server, not just in the screen.

question_examples: Why can't I edit a task?
Why is the project read-only for me?
Why are the edit buttons missing?
answer_rules: Explain that editing depends on project role, project status, and assignment.
Tell the user to ask a Project Manager or admin to confirm role and status.
Mention that permissions are server-enforced, not just UI.
forbidden_claims: All users can edit any project field.
BTPM lets viewers change project data.

articles.title: Why can't I generate a PowerPoint or status deck?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Common reasons: missing source data, wrong filters, no SharePoint output setup, missing permission, or a generation error.
articles.summary: Checklist for when project or roadmap deck generation does not work.
articles.body:
If a PowerPoint or status deck does not generate, the issue is usually missing source data, the wrong filters, a missing output setup, or a permission gap.

What to check

- Source data is present. Decks are generated from project and roadmap information already in BTPM. If key fields are empty, the deck cannot be built.
- Filters and scope. On the Roadmap, the deck reflects the selected workspace, program, and project filters. If the selection is empty, the deck cannot be generated.
- Output destination. SharePoint output must be configured for your project or workspace. If the folder link is missing or broken, generation will fail or have nowhere to publish.
- Your role. Generating an official deck usually requires a Project Manager, Workspace Admin, or Org Admin role depending on the deck type.
- A previous generation error. The Generated Documents area may show the last failure reason.

What to do next

- Update the missing project information first, then try again.
- Adjust roadmap filters to include the projects you expect.
- Ask an admin to confirm the SharePoint folder link and your role.

What BTPM will not do

BTPM will not invent missing project data to fill the deck. The output reflects what is in BTPM at generation time.

question_examples: Why can't I generate a PowerPoint?
Why does the status deck not export?
Why does my roadmap deck fail to generate?
answer_rules: List source data, filters, SharePoint setup, permission, and last error as the main checks.
Tell users to update BTPM data before retrying.
Explain decks are downstream outputs that reflect current BTPM state.
forbidden_claims: BTPM can generate a deck without any project data.
Decks are stored as the source of truth.

articles.title: Why is my Roadmap deck showing the wrong projects?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Roadmap decks reflect the workspace, program, and project filters at generation time. Old decks do not refresh automatically.
articles.summary: Practical reasons the Roadmap deck does not match what you expect to see.
articles.body:
Roadmap decks are generated from the current Roadmap view, including its filters and scope. If the deck shows the wrong projects, it is usually because of filters, scope, or stale generation.

What to check

- Active Roadmap filters. The deck includes only what the Roadmap shows when you generate it. Workspace, program, and project filters all matter.
- The selected workspace. If the wrong workspace (or "All workspaces") is selected, the deck may include or exclude the wrong projects.
- Project data freshness. Decks are snapshots. If a project was updated after the deck was generated, the deck will not reflect the change until you regenerate it.
- Archived or inactive projects. These are typically excluded by the Roadmap view and therefore by the deck.

What to do next

- Adjust the Roadmap filters so the view shows the projects you want in the deck.
- Confirm the workspace selection.
- Regenerate the deck after updating data or filters.

What BTPM will not do

BTPM will not silently rebuild old decks when project data changes. You must regenerate to get a fresh version.

question_examples: Why is the wrong project in my roadmap deck?
Why is my roadmap deck out of date?
Why is a project missing from the roadmap deck?
answer_rules: Explain that the deck uses current Roadmap filters and scope.
Tell users to adjust filters, confirm workspace, and regenerate.
Mention that old decks do not refresh automatically.
forbidden_claims: Roadmap decks update themselves after generation.
Filters do not affect the deck content.

articles.title: Why is Power BI data stale or different from BTPM?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Differences usually reflect Import refresh timing, Workspace reporting scope, report filters, the published report version, or source data not yet saved in BTPM.
articles.summary: Why Power BI may not match BTPM: Import refresh timing, Workspace scope, filters, published report version, or unsaved source data.
articles.body:
BTPM is the source of truth. Power BI is a downstream Import reporting layer.

What to check

- Confirm the source record is saved in BTPM.
- Confirm the Workspace is included under Admin → Power BI.
- Compare equivalent report filters and reporting periods on both sides.
- Check whether the imported report data is current (Import refresh timing).
- Check which published report version is being viewed.

Refresh model

- BTPM does not initiate or schedule Power BI refreshes.
- Where automated Power BI Service refresh is unavailable, use: Desktop Refresh → Save → Publish/Replace.
- Automated Power BI Service refresh requires the appropriate gateway/certificate arrangement where direct cloud connectivity is not available.

What BTPM will not do

- Power BI cannot write data back into BTPM.
- Source corrections must be made in BTPM.

question_examples: Why is Power BI data stale?
Why is Power BI different from BTPM?
Why don't my BTPM updates show in Power BI?
answer_rules: Explain the downstream boundary: BTPM is the source of truth and Power BI is a downstream Import reporting layer.
Check BTPM source data, Workspace scope under Admin → Power BI, report filters, and Import refresh freshness.
State that BTPM neither refreshes Power BI nor accepts Power BI write-back.
Where Power BI Service automated refresh is unavailable, mention Desktop Refresh → Save → Publish/Replace.
forbidden_claims: Power BI is the source of truth for BTPM data.
Power BI can change BTPM records.
BTPM refreshes or schedules Power BI.
A BTPM admin can refresh Power BI from BTPM.
Users should wait for the next BTPM sync.

articles.title: Why is a KPI App report not ready?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: A KPI App report is not ready when mapping, period, value/history, or snapshot readiness is incomplete.
articles.summary: Admin checklist for why a KPI is not ready to be sent to the external KPI App.
articles.body:
A KPI being "not ready" for the external KPI App usually means a setup or data condition is missing in BTPM. The admin monitor surfaces the specific reason.

What to check

- KPI mapping. The KPI must be mapped to the external KPI App (external KPI ID, scenario, currency, frequency, carry-forward rule, active state).
- Reporting period. The current reporting period must apply to this KPI. Off-cycle KPIs will not be ready outside their period.
- Value and history. The KPI needs an official snapshot for the period, or a valid carry-forward source if carry-forward is allowed.
- Validation messages. The readiness monitor lists the specific blocking reasons (missing mapping, missing snapshot, inactive mapping, etc.).

What to do next

- Open the KPI App admin monitor to see the specific reason for this KPI and period.
- Update the mapping or capture the missing snapshot in BTPM, then re-check readiness.
- Confirm the project and KPI are still active and assigned to the right scenario.

What BTPM will not do

BTPM will not invent a missing value, change KPI source truth, or mark a KPI as ready when blocking conditions are unresolved.

question_examples: Why is my KPI App report not ready?
Why is the KPI showing not ready?
What blocks a KPI from being reportable?
answer_rules: List mapping, reporting period, value/history, and validation messages as the main checks.
Tell admins to use the KPI App admin monitor to see the exact blocking reason.
Confirm BTPM remains the KPI source of truth.
forbidden_claims: BTPM will create a KPI value when none exists.
Power BI can fill in missing KPI snapshots for the KPI App.

articles.title: Why did KPI App submission fail?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: KPI App submissions fail on readiness gaps, mapping errors, payload issues, or external endpoint errors. Check the admin monitor first.
articles.summary: Admin troubleshooting for failed KPI App submissions.
articles.body:
A failed KPI App submission usually points to a readiness gap, a mapping problem, a payload issue, or an external endpoint error. The admin monitor records what happened.

What to check

- Readiness. Was the KPI actually ready at submission time? An unready KPI cannot be submitted.
- Mapping. The external KPI ID, scenario, currency, frequency, and active state must be correct and current.
- Payload. The outbox shows the payload built by BTPM. Validation messages explain payload issues.
- External endpoint. Errors from MuleSoft or the external KPI App (timeouts, rejections, authentication issues) are recorded against the submission.
- Retry status. Some failures are retried automatically; others require admin action.

What to do next

- Open the KPI App admin monitor and review the failed submission.
- Fix the underlying issue (readiness, mapping, or external setup), then retry the submission.
- If the external endpoint or admin setup is broken, contact the integration admin before retrying.

What BTPM will not do

BTPM will not change the KPI source value to make a submission succeed. The KPI source of truth stays in BTPM. Submissions reflect what is reportable, not a different version.

question_examples: Why did my KPI App submission fail?
Why is the KPI outbox showing an error?
What should I do when a KPI submission fails?
answer_rules: List readiness, mapping, payload, external endpoint, and retry as the main checks.
Tell admins to use the KPI App monitor to see the exact error.
State that BTPM does not change KPI source values to make a submission succeed.
forbidden_claims: BTPM will overwrite KPI values to make submissions succeed.
Failed submissions update the external KPI App anyway.

articles.title: Why is BTPM Guide not answering my question?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: BTPM Guide answers only from Knowledge Center articles. If coverage is missing or the question is unclear, it will say so.
articles.summary: Why BTPM Guide may not answer and how to get a better answer.
articles.body:
BTPM Guide answers questions about BTPM using the Knowledge Center as its source. If it does not answer, the cause is usually missing coverage, unclear wording, or an out-of-scope question.

What to check

- The question is about BTPM. BTPM Guide does not answer questions outside BTPM (travel, general business advice, unrelated tools).
- The wording is clear. Short, direct questions get better answers ("How do I add a risk?" rather than a vague topic).
- The Knowledge Center has an article for the topic. If no article exists, BTPM Guide will say it does not have enough information.
- You are not asking for operational data. BTPM Guide does not read project risks, KPI values, SharePoint files, or user records.

What to do next

- Rephrase the question more directly.
- Open the Knowledge Center and search for the topic.
- Ask an admin to add or improve the article if coverage is missing.

What BTPM will not do

BTPM Guide will not invent an answer when no Knowledge Center content covers it.

question_examples: Why is BTPM Guide not answering me?
Why does BTPM Guide say it doesn't know?
Why is the assistant not giving me an answer?
answer_rules: Explain BTPM Guide is Knowledge Center-only and does not read operational data.
Tell users to rephrase, check the Knowledge Center, or ask an admin to add an article.
State that out-of-scope questions will not be answered.
forbidden_claims: BTPM Guide can read operational project data.
BTPM Guide answers questions outside BTPM.

articles.title: Why does BTPM Guide say it does not have enough information?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: BTPM Guide says this when no Knowledge Center article covers the question or when the question asks for operational data it cannot read.
articles.summary: What it means when BTPM Guide replies that it doesn't have enough information.
articles.body:
When BTPM Guide says it does not have enough information, it is being honest rather than guessing. There are two common reasons.

What to check

- The Knowledge Center does not have an article covering the question yet. BTPM Guide only answers from Knowledge Center content.
- The question asks for live operational content — project risks, KPI values, specific tasks, SharePoint file contents, user records. BTPM Guide does not read this data in the current version.
- The wording is too broad. A more specific question often matches an existing article.

What to do next

- Try a more specific question ("How do I generate a project status deck?" rather than "reporting").
- Open the Knowledge Center and look for the topic directly.
- For operational answers (status, values, files), use the relevant BTPM page, not BTPM Guide.
- Ask an admin to add a Knowledge Center article if a topic is missing.

What BTPM will not do

BTPM Guide will not fabricate an answer when there is no source. It will say it doesn't have enough information instead.

question_examples: Why does BTPM Guide say it doesn't have enough information?
Why does the assistant say it doesn't know?
How do I get BTPM Guide to answer a missing topic?
answer_rules: Explain BTPM Guide is Knowledge Center-only and refuses to guess.
Tell users to rephrase, search the Knowledge Center, or ask an admin to add content.
State that operational data is not available through BTPM Guide.
forbidden_claims: BTPM Guide will guess when content is missing.
BTPM Guide can read operational project data on demand.

articles.title: Why are sources shown but the answer is weak?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Weak answers with sources usually mean the articles match loosely or the content is too thin. Improve the Knowledge Center article wording and metadata.
articles.summary: Admin guidance when BTPM Guide returns sources but the answer is not helpful.
articles.body:
When BTPM Guide shows sources but the answer is weak, the retrieval found loosely related articles or the articles are not specific enough. This is a content quality signal, not a retrieval bug.

What to check

- Article wording. Does the matched article actually answer the user's question directly? If it only mentions related concepts, the answer will be vague.
- Article metadata. Synonyms, user intents, and question examples help retrieval find the right article. Missing or generic metadata reduces precision.
- Coverage gaps. Sometimes the right article doesn't exist yet and a related one is picked instead.
- Evaluation protocol. The BTPM Guide Evaluation page records the actual sources and scores per question and helps identify weak matches.

What to do next

- Open the matched article and improve the body to answer the question directly.
- Add or refine synonyms, question examples, and answer rules in the article metadata.
- Add a new, more specific article if coverage is missing.
- Rerun BTPM Guide Evaluation to confirm the change.

What BTPM will not do

BTPM Guide will not improve answers by guessing beyond the Knowledge Center. Better answers come from better KC content.

question_examples: Why are the sources shown but the answer is weak?
Why does BTPM Guide cite the wrong article?
How do I improve a weak BTPM Guide answer?
answer_rules: Explain weak answers usually reflect article wording or metadata, not a retrieval bug.
Tell admins to improve article body, synonyms, question examples, and answer rules.
Mention BTPM Guide Evaluation as the way to verify improvements.
forbidden_claims: BTPM Guide can produce strong answers without Knowledge Center coverage.
Retrieval changes alone will fix vague articles.

articles.title: How should admins use BTPM Guide Evaluation?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Use BTPM Guide Evaluation to batch-run curated and metadata-derived questions, review pass/warn/fail outcomes, and download a protocol.
articles.summary: Practical guide for admins running BTPM Guide Evaluation.
articles.body:
BTPM Guide Evaluation lets Org Admins batch-test BTPM Guide answers without going through one question at a time.

What it does

- Runs a question bank against BTPM Guide using the same retrieval and prompts as normal use.
- Scores each answer as pass, warn, or fail based on expected behavior, expected sources, required points, and forbidden claims.
- Lets you download a JSON protocol of the full run for review.

Question banks

- Curated bank: a fixed set of representative questions covering core BTPM topics.
- Metadata-derived bank: questions generated from Knowledge Center article metadata to widen coverage.
- Combined run: both banks together.

How to use it

1. Open Admin and go to BTPM Guide Evaluation.
2. Choose a bank and a run size (start with a small run to validate setup).
3. Start the run and let it complete. Cancel if you need to stop early.
4. Review the pass/warn/fail summary and inspect individual results.
5. Download the protocol for record-keeping or content review.

What to do with results

- Pass: behavior matched expectations.
- Warn: minor mismatch (loose sources, missing supporting points) — review whether the article needs improvement.
- Fail: a real gap. Improve article content or metadata, then rerun.

Responsible use

Large runs send many API calls to the BTPM Guide provider. Use a reasonable size, especially during initial tuning. The evaluation never persists answers and never reads operational project data.

question_examples: How do admins use BTPM Guide Evaluation?
What is the BTPM Guide Evaluation page?
How should I run BTPM Guide tests?
answer_rules: Explain curated, metadata-derived, and combined banks.
Walk through running, reviewing pass/warn/fail, and downloading the protocol.
Mention responsible API usage and that no operational data is read.
forbidden_claims: Evaluation reads live operational project data.
Evaluation answers are persisted to the database.

articles.title: Can BTPM automatically approve KPI submissions?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: BTPM can support controlled KPI submission workflows, but it should not silently approve KPI submissions for you.
articles.summary: BTPM helps admins prepare, validate, monitor, and submit KPI information through the KPI App integration. Approval and submission must follow the configured admin process and should not be treated as an automatic AI action.

question_examples: Can BTPM automatically approve KPI submissions?
Does BTPM approve KPI reports by itself?
Can BTPM Guide approve a KPI submission?
Can the KPI App submit missing KPI values automatically?
answer_rules: Say BTPM should not silently approve KPI submissions.
Explain that submission must follow the configured admin process.
State that BTPM Guide cannot approve or submit a KPI for the user.
Tell admins to fix source KPI setup or values in BTPM first.
forbidden_claims: BTPM Guide can approve KPI submissions.
BTPM can invent missing KPI values.
KPI App submission replaces KPI validation.

articles.title: Are exported reports the live project record?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Exported reports, decks, and charters are snapshots. BTPM remains the live project record.
articles.summary: Generated reports are useful for communication, but they do not become the live source of truth. Update BTPM first, then regenerate the output when needed.

question_examples: Can I treat exported reports as the live project record?
Is the PowerPoint deck the source of truth?
Does editing an exported report update BTPM?
Should I maintain project status in Excel or PowerPoint?
answer_rules: Say exported reports are snapshots, not the live record.
State that BTPM remains the source of truth.
Tell users to update BTPM first and regenerate outputs.
Warn against maintaining a separate manual truth in exported files.
forbidden_claims: Exported reports are the live project record.
Editing PowerPoint updates BTPM.
Users should maintain project truth outside BTPM.

articles.title: How do I request access for another user?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: BTPM Guide cannot grant access, but it can explain who should request or approve access.
articles.summary: If another user needs access, follow the proper access path. BTPM Guide cannot grant access or bypass permissions.
articles.body:
BTPM Guide cannot grant access for another user.

If someone needs access to a project, workspace, file, or admin area, the request should go through the proper owner or admin path.

What to do:

1. Identify what access is needed: project, workspace, SharePoint folder, Power BI workspace, or admin page.
2. Confirm why the person needs access.
3. Ask the Project Manager, Workspace Admin, Org Admin, or file owner to grant the right access.
4. If the access is for SharePoint or Power BI, remember that Microsoft permissions may need to be managed outside BTPM.
5. Ask the user to refresh or sign in again after access is granted.

Do not share links as a workaround for missing access. A link does not replace permission.

BTPM Guide can explain how access normally works, but it cannot add a user, change a role, invite someone, or bypass permission rules.

question_examples: How do I request access for Petya?
Can BTPM Guide give someone access?
Who can grant project access?
What should I do if someone cannot open a project?
answer_rules: State that BTPM Guide cannot grant access.
Tell users to identify the access type first.
Direct users to the proper owner/admin path.
Mention SharePoint and Power BI permissions may be managed outside BTPM.
forbidden_claims: BTPM Guide can grant access.
Sharing a link bypasses permissions.
Project access automatically grants SharePoint or Power BI access.

articles.title: What can BTPM Guide do for me?
articles.tooltip_excerpt: BTPM Guide explains how to use BTPM, but it does not perform actions or read private project data.
articles.summary: BTPM Guide can help you understand BTPM pages, concepts, workflows, and limitations. It cannot create records, update data, read operational project content, or bypass access.

question_examples: What can BTPM Guide do for me?
What can BTPM Guide not do?
Can BTPM Guide create tasks?
Can BTPM Guide read my project data?
Can BTPM Guide approve KPI submissions?
answer_rules: Explain BTPM Guide as a help assistant.
Clearly distinguish explanation from action.
State that BTPM Guide cannot read operational project data or perform mutations.
Give examples of useful question wording.
For change management questions, prefer Adoption Plan articles unless the user clearly asks about formal Change Control or Change Request approvals.
forbidden_claims: BTPM Guide can create or update records.
BTPM Guide can read private project data.
BTPM Guide can bypass permissions.

articles.title: Using the Project Calendar
articles.tooltip_excerpt: The Project Calendar helps users see project dates, milestones, governance events, and upcoming time-based items.
articles.summary: Use the Project Calendar to understand what is coming up inside one project. It helps with date visibility, but it does not replace the project plan, Gantt, or Outlook calendar.
articles.body:
The Project Calendar shows time-based project information in one place.

Use it when you want to understand upcoming dates for a specific project, such as milestones, task due dates, governance events, or other scheduled project items depending on the setup.

What to do here:

1. Review upcoming project dates.
2. Check whether important milestones or reviews are visible.
3. Look for overdue or missing items.
4. Open the related task, phase, governance record, or project area for details.
5. Update the source item in BTPM if something is wrong.

The Project Calendar is a visibility tool. It does not replace the project plan, Gantt, or Outlook calendar.

Use Gantt when you need to understand project sequencing and timeline logic. Use Outlook or Teams for meeting invites. Use BTPM Calendar to understand project-related dates and follow-up.

question_examples: What should I use the Project Calendar for?
How is Project Calendar different from Gantt?
Does the Project Calendar replace Outlook?
What dates should I check here?
answer_rules: Explain Project Calendar as project date visibility.
Distinguish it from Gantt and Outlook.
Tell users to update the source item in BTPM if a date is wrong.
forbidden_claims: Project Calendar replaces Outlook meetings.
Project Calendar is the project plan.
Calendar edits automatically fix all source items.

articles.title: Using Programs
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Programs help group related projects so teams can review a broader initiative or portfolio outcome.
articles.summary: Use Programs when several projects contribute to the same business outcome. A program groups projects; it does not replace project-level execution.
articles.body:
Programs help group related projects.

Use a program when several projects contribute to a broader initiative, portfolio, transformation area, or business outcome. The program gives users a way to look above individual projects without losing the project-level execution detail.

What to do here:

1. Review which projects belong together.
2. Use a program when the grouping helps reporting or governance.
3. Keep project execution inside each project.
4. Use the program view to understand the broader picture.
5. Avoid creating programs that do not help users make decisions.

A program is not the same as a project. A project has its own owner, plan, risks, blockers, KPIs, and governance. A program groups projects so the organization can see progress across them.

Do not use programs as a dumping ground. If projects are unrelated, they should not be grouped just to make the list shorter.

question_examples: What is a program in BTPM?
When should I use a program?
Is a program the same as a project?
How should projects be grouped?
answer_rules: Explain program as a grouping of related projects.
State that project execution remains in projects.
Warn against grouping unrelated projects.
forbidden_claims: A program replaces project execution.
Every project must belong to a program.
Programs should be used as dumping grounds.

articles.title: Using Workspace Members
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Workspace Members helps users understand who belongs to the workspace and where access or role checks may be needed.
articles.summary: Use Workspace Members to review who is connected to a workspace. Workspace membership helps with visibility, but project, SharePoint, and Power BI permissions may still apply separately.
articles.body:
Workspace Members shows people connected to a workspace.

Use it when you need to understand who belongs to the workspace, who may need access, or whether a user's workspace context looks correct.

What to check:

1. Is the user part of the right workspace?
2. What role do they have?
3. Do they also need access to a specific project?
4. Do they need SharePoint or Power BI permission outside BTPM?
5. Should access be removed when the person no longer needs it?

Workspace membership is important, but it does not always grant access to everything. A user may still need project-level access, SharePoint folder permission, or Power BI workspace permission.

BTPM Guide cannot add or remove workspace members. An authorized admin must manage user and workspace access through the proper process.

question_examples: What is the Members tab for?
Does workspace membership grant project access?
Why can't a workspace member see a project?
Can BTPM Guide add a member?
answer_rules: Explain Workspace Members as workspace membership visibility.
Clarify that project, SharePoint, and Power BI permissions may still apply.
State BTPM Guide cannot add or remove members.
forbidden_claims: Workspace membership grants every project automatically.
BTPM Guide can add workspace members.
SharePoint and Power BI permissions are always inherited from BTPM.

articles.title: Using Admin Invitations
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Admin Invitations helps admins invite users and check whether onboarding or access setup still needs attention.
articles.summary: Use Admin Invitations to manage user invitations into BTPM. Invitations help start access, but final visibility may still depend on role, workspace, project, and external permissions.
articles.body:
Admin Invitations is where admins manage user invitations into BTPM.

Use this area when a new user needs to join, when an invitation needs to be checked, or when someone says they cannot access the app after being invited.

What to check:

1. Was the invitation sent to the correct email address?
2. Has the user accepted it?
3. Is the user using the correct account?
4. Is the user assigned to the right organization or workspace?
5. Does the user need project-level access?
6. Does the user also need SharePoint or Power BI access?

An invitation starts the access process. It does not automatically mean the user can see every project, file, report, or admin page.

If a user cannot access what they need after accepting an invitation, check role, workspace, project access, and external Microsoft permissions.

BTPM Guide can explain the invitation process, but it cannot invite users or change access.

articles.body:
If you cannot access BTPM, start with the basics.

What to check:

1. Are you using the correct email account?
2. Have you accepted the invitation?

articles.title: Project Delivery Model rulebook
articles.tooltip_excerpt: Delivery Model is a project classification field: Internal Delivery, Vendor Delivery, Co-delivery, or Unclassified.
articles.summary: Delivery Model is a project classification field: Internal Delivery, Vendor Delivery, Co-delivery, or Unclassified.
articles.body:
Delivery Model classifies how a project is delivered. It is not project status, not project stage, not health, and not lifecycle.

Current values are:
- **Internal Delivery**: the work is delivered mainly by internal teams.
- **Vendor Delivery**: the work is delivered mainly by an external vendor.
- **Co-delivery**: internal and vendor teams jointly deliver the work.
- **Unclassified**: no delivery model has been selected yet.

The Delivery Model appears in the project identity header as `Delivery: ...`, can be selected when creating a new project, and can be changed in the project Edit dialog.

Use Delivery Model to classify responsibility and delivery setup. Do not use it to signal whether the project is late, blocked, active, or healthy.

articles.title: Stage, Status, Health, Lifecycle, and Delivery Model
articles.tooltip_excerpt: BTPM separates five axes: stage, workflow status, health, lifecycle, and delivery model.
articles.summary: BTPM separates five axes: stage, workflow status, health, lifecycle, and delivery model.
articles.body:
BTPM deliberately separates several concepts that are often confused:

- **Stage**: delivery phase concept: Initiation, Planning, Execution, Closure.
- **Status**: workflow state: Not Started, In Progress, On Hold, Completed, Cancelled.
- **Health**: derived delivery judgment shown in reporting, separate from status.
- **Lifecycle**: Active or Archived for business objects. Archived objects are hidden/limited but preserved unless permanently deleted by an authorized admin flow.
- **Delivery Model**: how the project is delivered: Internal Delivery, Vendor Delivery, Co-delivery, or Unclassified.

Do not merge these concepts. A project can be in Execution stage, In Progress status, At Risk health, Active lifecycle, and Vendor Delivery model at the same time.

BTPM is the live project record. Power BI dashboards, SharePoint files, generated PowerPoint decks, and exports are downstream or supporting outputs.

Dependencies remain same-level sequencing only. A dependency is not the same as a risk or a blocker.

articles.summary: The Projects module contains Projects, Programs, Templates, Members, and SharePoint tabs for the active workspace.
articles.body:
The canonical Projects module is opened from the left navigation. It is scoped by the active workspace.

Tabs:
- **Projects**: list, search, filter, group, sort, saved views, and create projects.
- **Programs**: create/open programs and show archived programs.
- **Templates**: view reusable project blueprints saved from projects.
- **Members**: manage workspace members where permitted.
- **SharePoint**: read-only workspace SharePoint library connection view. Admin configuration lives under Admin → SharePoint.

If the page says “Select a workspace to use Projects,” choose a specific workspace from the main workspace selector.

Adoption Plan is the project area for people-side readiness and adoption work.

Inside Adoption Plan there are two sub-tabs:
- Plan: the current project-specific Adoption Plan. Before generation it shows an empty state. After generation it shows the overview, Adoption tasks grouped by initiative, Manage adoption links, and linked risks/blockers/KPIs.
- Templates: the reusable template workspace. Before generation it is used to generate the Adoption Plan from the Standard or a custom template. After generation it is used to manage templates and add selected tasks from a template into the existing Adoption Plan.

Generated Adoption tasks are normal Planning tasks. Existing tasks, risks, blockers, and KPIs can be linked to the Adoption Plan and remain editable in their normal views.

articles.title: BTPM main workflows overview
articles.tooltip_excerpt: BTPM workflows move from setup and planning into execution, governance, reporting, and integrations.
articles.summary: Use this onboarding overview to understand the main workflow areas in BTPM: setup, portfolio structure, project planning, execution tracking, delivery control, governance, reporting, and integrations.
articles.body:
BTPM is organized around a simple operating flow: set up the workspace, structure the work, execute the work, govern delivery, and report from the same source data.

The core hierarchy is Organization > Workspace > Program > Project > Phase > Task. Organization and Workspace define where people work and what they can see. Programs group related projects. Projects are the main delivery streams. Phases break a project into major stages. Tasks are the executable work items inside phases.

The main BTPM workflow areas are:

1. Setup and access. Admins create or manage the organization, workspaces, users, invitations, workspace membership, and roles. This controls who can see and update work.

2. Portfolio and program setup. Teams group related work into programs, create projects in the correct workspace, assign owners, classify projects, and define major sequencing or dependencies.

3. Project setup and planning. Project leads define the project basics, scope, delivery model, dates, team, KPIs, phases, tasks, owners, and dependencies. This is where work becomes structured enough to execute and report.

4. Execution tracking. Assignees and project leads update tasks and phases, record dated execution updates, add comments where discussion or context is needed, and keep status/progress information current.

5. Delivery control. Teams manage dependencies, risks, and blockers. A risk is a potential future issue. A blocker is a current impediment that is already preventing progress. Dependencies explain sequencing between related pieces of work.

6. Governance and evidence. Project teams use governance cadence, governance records, decisions, evidence, health reviews, blocker reviews, dependency reviews, KPI updates, and status snapshots to keep management review traceable.

7. Reporting and roadmap visibility. BTPM derives reporting from the structured project data. Roadmap, dashboards, timelines, calendars, generated PowerPoint decks, KPI views, and Power BI outputs are downstream reporting surfaces. They should not become separate manual versions of the truth.

8. Files and integrations. BTPM can connect supporting files, SharePoint folders, exports, imports, Power BI, KPI App, and generated documents where configured. These support the project record, but the live project structure and execution record remain in BTPM.

For a new user, the best way to understand BTPM is to start with the hierarchy, then learn the workflow area that matches the job they need to do. For example: create a project, plan phases and tasks, update execution, manage a blocker, record governance evidence, review the Roadmap, or generate a status deck.

BTPM Guide can explain these areas and point users to relevant Knowledge Center articles or verified workflows. It should not turn this overview into one arbitrary workflow such as KPI App Report Now, project creation, task creation, or a generated document flow unless the user explicitly asks for that specific workflow.

Adoption and readiness workflow

For projects that need people-side readiness work, BTPM includes an Adoption Plan workflow.

The Adoption Plan workflow helps project teams structure stakeholder impact, communication, training, feedback, adoption tracking, hypercare, and reinforcement work.

The workflow is:
1. Open Project → Adoption Plan.
2. Use Templates to select the BTPM Standard Adoption Template or a custom workspace template.
3. Generate one Adoption Plan for the project.
4. Manage the generated Adoption tasks in Planning.
5. Link existing tasks, risks, blockers, and KPIs to the Adoption Plan where relevant.
6. After the plan exists, use Templates to manage reusable templates or add selected new tasks from a template into the existing Adoption Plan.

Adoption Plan follows the BTPM source-of-truth model. Generated and added work becomes normal BTPM phases and tasks. Linked risks, blockers, and KPIs remain normal BTPM objects. Templates are reusable structures, not execution records.

Users may call this change management or change readiness. In BTPM, the feature name is Adoption Plan. It is not formal Change Control or a Change Request approval workflow.
